2611.28319.authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
2611.28319.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

2611.28346.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
2611.28346.authors: Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu
2611.28346.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

2611.28403.title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
2611.28403.authors: Jiahao Wang, Chaehyeon Song, Dongjiao He, Jan Quenzel, Lintong Zhang, Ayoung Kim, Maurice Fallon
2611.28403.abstract: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

2611.28508.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
2611.28508.authors: Yuxiang Wei, Zundong Wu, Weiyu Sun, Qizhen Lan, Yanteng Zhang, Vince D. Calhoun
2611.28508.abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

2611.28509.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
2611.28509.authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Weisong Shi
2611.28509.abstract: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.

2611.28532.title: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories
2611.28532.authors: Enguang Fan, Binh Minh Tran, Fulin Wang, Jiaxi Li, Klara Nahrstedt
2611.28532.abstract: Everyday smartphone walks offer a scalable source of indoor geometry, but their motion traces drift and their radio measurements are distorted by multipath. We present Walks2Maps, a physics-guided framework that reconstructs a shared metric map from Wi-Fi round-trip-time (RTT) and motion observations, without a floor plan, surveyed access-point (AP) coordinates, or position labels. Walks2Maps jointly estimates pedestrian trajectories, AP locations, and per-trajectory stride scales, then recovers the pathway layout from the reconstructed paths. Shared AP observations connect walks recorded in different local frames, while metric ranges constrain their relative geometry and scale. An asymmetric range loss accommodates multipath-induced excess delay. On 22 phone trajectories collected along 11 routes on an office floor with 30 APs, Walks2Maps achieves median AP and trajectory errors of 0.87 m and 0.89 m, respectively, and a walked-area F1 score of 0.985. Ablations show that radio similarity can recognize places while still producing a distorted map; retaining the metric information in RTT resolves this ambiguity. Asymmetric modeling further reduces AP error by 54% relative to a symmetric loss. These results demonstrate how radio and motion measurements can jointly reveal indoor geometry without a dedicated mapping survey. We will release the dataset and toolkit.

2611.28573.title: MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models
2611.28573.authors: Tirtho Roy, Shreyan Ganguly, Muhammad Arbab Arshad, Nikhil Bhattacharya, Soumik Sarkar
2611.28573.abstract: In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections. Retrieved disease labels accounted for most of the gain, and adding the corresponding text descriptions improved in-distribution accuracy by about six percentage points.

2611.28612.title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
2611.28612.authors: Yifei Cheng, Xiaolin Zhang, Yu-Xuan Qiu
2611.28612.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.

2611.28745.title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
2611.28745.authors: Jianxin Gao, Bohan Chen, Runze Li, Qi Zhang
2611.28745.abstract: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

2611.28768.title: A high-speed and high-resolution 3D velocity map imaging system with a neuromorphic camera
2611.28768.authors: Sulaiman Abubakar, Blessed Oguh, Akaninyene Udoikono, Hackim Musah, Suk Kyoung Lee, Wen Li
2611.28768.abstract: An improved camera-based 3D-velocity map imaging (VMI) system was demonstrated with a neuromorphic camera. We show a machine vision event-driven camera can achieve an unprecedented latency of 2 microseconds when detecting single ion/electron with a microchannel plate imaging detector, which boosts the speed of the momentum imaging system to more than 100 kHz, while the system with a conventional frame camera is limited to a few kHz. The high spatial resolution of the camera offers additional performance boost while maintaining excellent multi-hit capability and a high time resolution.

2611.28793.title: STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
2611.28793.authors: Boyi Zhu, Youcheng Cai, Dong Wang
2611.28793.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

2611.28809.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
2611.28809.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

2611.28943.title: SANA-Robot: Efficient World Action Model with Hybrid Memory
2611.28943.authors: Yuyang Zhao, Zekai Li, Yicheng Pan, Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Jiaxu Xing, Moritz Reuss, Quanquan Peng, Junsong Chen, Enze Xie, Zhijian Liu, Song Han
2611.28943.abstract: World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/

2611.28947.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
2611.28947.authors: Jiaqi Su, Jie-Jing Shao, Yichen Liu, Long-Kai Huang, Haiyan Yin
2611.28947.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

2611.28978.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
2611.28978.authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
2611.28978.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.

2611.29027.title: 3D-EMCAD: Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoding for Volumetric Brain Tumor Segmentation
2611.29027.authors: Iftakhar Hossain, Israt Jahan Sinthia, Md. Hadiur Rahman Khan
2611.29027.abstract: Encoder-decoder networks are widely used for volumetric brain tumor segmentation, yet recent trends favor high-capacity decoders that incur steep computational costs in 3D at high spatial resolutions. The Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoder (EMCAD) is a lightweight decoder that achieves strong accuracy at very low cost, but it has been validated only in 2D. Here, we extend EMCAD to volumetric segmentation (3D-EMCAD) by converting all operations to 3D and replacing standard normalization layers with group normalization to suit the small batch sizes of volumetric training. To isolate the impact of decoder choice, we evaluate five decoders: the proposed 3D-EMCAD, a vanilla SegResNet decoder, an Attention U-Net decoder, UNet++, and a plain U-Net decoder using an identical 3D SegResNet encoder and training protocol on BraTS 2020 (369 cases, three-fold cross-validation). The five decoders yield statistically indistinguishable performance: their mean Dice scores span only 0.0071, less than the fold-to-fold variation of most models, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows no significant difference between 3D-EMCAD and three of the four baselines. Importantly, 3D-EMCAD achieves this shared accuracy with the fewest decoder parameters (1.15 M) and operations (8.6 G), requiring $7.3\times$ fewer operations than UNet++, which scores no higher. These findings demonstrate that decoder capacity beyond a modest budget offers no measurable benefit for volumetric brain tumor segmentation.

2611.29057.title: DiRGeo: Learning Directional Geometry of Visual Representations
2611.29057.abstract: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.

2611.29116.title: A Camera-Based Single-Volume, Monolithic Compton Camera
2611.29116.authors: Alex Bocchieri, Devanshi Jain, Andreas Velten
2611.29116.abstract: A Compton camera measures two events in a detector from individual gamma-rays to reconstruct the radiation source. Conventional scintillator-based Compton cameras consist of two separate scintillator volumes or a single segmented scintillator, resulting in drawbacks regarding detector bulkiness and efficiency. Their scintillator readout techniques struggle to resolve two nearby events in one monolithic scintillator. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras have recently been proposed for measuring scintillation events in various configurations. SPAD array sensors enable high-resolution photon-counting acquisition at high rates that is easily scalable to millions of pixels. Prior work has explored different optics and measurement arrangements as well as demonstrated measurement of single interaction locations. In this work, we extend these capabilities to demonstrate a practical radiation imaging device in the form of a Compton camera consisting of a SPAD camera and one compact, monolithic scintillator. Our Compton camera prototype successfully reconstructs a gamma-ray source over multiple locations that span a 4$\pi$ steradian field of view. Our approach is able to resolve two simultaneous events in one monolithic scintillator and enables Compton camera devices with compact, monolithic scintillator volumes for enhanced portability.

2611.29154.title: MVAgent: Per-Video Agents under Global Coordination for Multi-Video Understanding
2611.29154.authors: Kewei Wei, XueXiang Wen, Bocheng Hu, Weili Xu, Haiyang Yu, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
2611.29154.abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.

2611.29205.title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
2611.29205.authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Zheyuan Lai, Liuxuan Sun, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
2611.29205.abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.

2611.29269.title: Dually Constrained Parameter Projection for Continual Learning
2611.29269.authors: Bowyn Tan, Zhilong Zheng, Yang Guan, Liming Xiao, Liye Tang, Xiao Li, Naizheng Wang, Keqiang Li, Shengbo Eben Li
2611.29269.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to learn multiple new tasks sequentially while retaining performance on previous tasks. Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.

2611.29277.title: $\zeta_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
2611.29277.authors: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang, Junyu Liu, Hongchu Zeng, Xinyi Peng, Chuxuan Huang, Yicheng Su, Zihao Zhou, Shengcheng Fu, Haoyang Li, Liyun Yan, Tianyue Zhan, Jianming Ma, Yang Zhang, Keqi Zhu, Xiaxi Si, Jinming Yao, Qiao Sun, Shizeng Zhang, Jiangwei Zhong, Yue Gao
2611.29277.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/

2611.29294.title: RSLaA: Self-Reconfiguring Roadside LiDARs as Agents for 3D Traffic Perception
2611.29294.authors: Yang Ma, Yichen Sun, Yubing Zheng, Zhongxiang Feng, Zeyang Cheng, Said M. Easa
2611.29294.abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.

2611.29339.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
2611.29339.authors: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao, Moyun Liu, Xingwei Zhao, Bo Tao, Jiawei Du, Joey Tianyi Zhou
2611.29339.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.

2611.29377.title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
2611.29377.authors: Shilin Shan, Yuxuan Hu, Chuhao Zhou, Yimeng Dong, Bohan Hou, Jiaqi Bai, Boyu Ma, Jiahua Dong, Jianfei Yang
2611.29377.abstract: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.

2611.29411.title: Who Plays What: Same-Instrument Music Separation from Video
2611.29411.authors: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Sebastiano Vascon, Dorien Herremans
2611.29411.abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.

2611.29494.title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
2611.29494.authors: Ewsey Obzherin, Samira Atlangirieva, Anastasia Antsiferova, Valentin Khrulkov, Art Prosvetov, Andrey Kuznetsov
2611.29494.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

2611.29507.title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
2611.29507.authors: Anubhav Pandey, Harshit Nagpal, Aditya Agarwal, Tejasvi Alladi, Fei Richard Yu
2611.29507.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.

2611.29558.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
2611.29558.authors: Haoxiang Zhan, Haoqin Hong, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
2611.29558.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.

2611.29658.title: How Reliable is AI-Generated Audio Description? A Multilingual Expert Evaluation
2611.29658.authors: Annette Rios, Lukas Fischer, Sarah Ebling
2611.29658.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.

2611.29734.title: Lightweight Spectral Subspace Filtering for Trojan-Resilient AI Inference Engines
2611.29734.authors: Soumita Chatterjee, Sudip Ghosh, Tamal Ghosh, Bhargab B. Bhattacharya, Hafizur Rahaman
2611.29734.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a training-free Spectral Subspace Filtering framework that detects and suppresses backdoor-induced activations by analyzing latent feature representations. Exploiting the geometric separation between benign and malicious feature distributions, the framework employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the dominant malicious subspace and performs inference-time spectral scrubbing through activation projection. This approach suppresses backdoor effects without model retraining, requiring only a small set of triggered samples collected offline. Experimental evaluation across CNN and transformer architectures, including AlexNet, ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNetV2, and Vision Transformer (ViT), demonstrates that the proposed method reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 94.2-99.8% to an average of 2.07%, while preserving clean accuracy of up to 98.54% with low inference overhead. The framework also demonstrates robustness across varying poisoning rates and multiple concurrent triggers, highlighting its potential as a lightweight runtime defense for enhancing the security and reliability of AI inference engines against backdoor attacks.

2611.29815.title: Model Immunization Cannot Reliably Protect Models from Harmful Adaptation
2611.29815.authors: Tong Li, Chenru Wang, Chris Thomas, Shengwei An
2611.29815.abstract: Efficient fine-tuning techniques have substantially reduced the cost of adapting open-weight models, enabling malicious actors to readily fine-tune them toward harmful capabilities. In response, model immunization modifies a pretrained checkpoint to resist subsequent adaptation toward designated harmful capabilities while preserving its utility and adaptability for benign tasks. Furthermore, a few immunization methods have sought to keep their protection robust to some changes in the attacker's adaptation. However, fine-tuning offers attackers many more low-cost options, and we observe that existing methods still substantially overfit to the attacker configuration they are optimized against. Such overfitting stays hidden when immunization is evaluated under, or near, this configuration, so the reported protection may give a false sense of security. To rigorously evaluate model immunization, we conduct experiments, varying one component of this configuration at a time: the harmful data, the adaptation strategy, or the model initialization. Across four immunization methods on text-to-image generation and image classification, with additional results on language models, these variations substantially degrade the protection, and in many cases the immunized model relearns the harmful capability nearly as well as the un-immunized model. Existing immunization therefore cannot reliably protect models, leaving them vulnerable to harmful adaptation.

2611.29874.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
2611.29874.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

2611.29897.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
2611.29897.authors: Yue Huang, Tianshan Zhang, Zeyu Zhang, Jayeon Kang, Akide Liu, Sungjoon Choi, Dacheng Tao, Hao Tang
2611.29897.abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

2611.29905.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
2611.29905.authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Li Combeau, Nicolas Michel, Toshihiko Yamasaki
2611.29905.abstract: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

2611.29914.title: Generalizable Variable-Rate Adaptation for Image Coding for Machines
2611.29914.abstract: Image Coding for Machines (ICM) aims to preserve task-relevant information for machine vision under limited bitrates. However, most ICM models are trained for a fixed operating point, and extending them to variable-rate compression is challenging because their training objectives differ across tasks and model designs. In this paper, we propose a loss-agnostic distillation framework for variable-rate ICM. A pretrained fixed-rate ICM model is used as a frozen teacher, while a student model learns variable-rate behavior through importance-adaptive quantization and distillation-based optimization. This enables continuous bitrate control with a single model while preserving task-relevant latent components, without requiring the original task-specific loss or downstream task labels. Experiments based on existing ICM models demonstrate that the proposed method provides continuous bitrate control and achieves competitive recognition performance compared with the fixed-rate models.

2611.29969.title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
2611.29969.authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
2611.29969.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

2611.30042.title: SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments
2611.30042.authors: Jenna Kang, Bingxuan Li, Colin Groth, Anatolii Evdokimov, Sai Zhang, Qi Sun
2611.30042.abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

2611.30050.title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
2611.30050.authors: Yasaman Mohammadpour, Pouya Shaeri, Ariane Middel
2611.30050.abstract: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $\rho = 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($\rho = -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

2611.30065.title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
2611.30065.authors: Hyungyu Lee, Saehyung Lee, Ho Bae, Sungroh Yoon
2611.30065.abstract: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.

2611.30099.title: Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
2611.30099.authors: Sunjae Jeong, Geunhyeok Yu, Dowoon Lee, Hyoseok Hwang
2611.30099.abstract: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.

2611.30101.title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
2611.30101.authors: Gengming Cui, Mingfei Han, Jiawei Zhang, Mozheng Liao, Yunkai Guo, Minghao Jin, Tingwen Du, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
2611.30101.abstract: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

2611.30149.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
2611.30149.authors: Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
2611.30149.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

2611.30288.title: Face Is Not All You Need: MIME Benchmark for Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition
2611.30288.authors: Yuxin Jia, Xing Lan, Wensong Wang, Jian Xue, Feiliang Ren, Ke Lu
2611.30288.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.

2611.30310.title: Seeing Together, Acting Apart: Shared Environmental Understanding for Multi-Robot Navigation
2611.30310.authors: Haihong Hao, Lei Chen, Mingfei Han, Chenglong Yan, Dong An, Yuqiang Yang, Changlin Li, Minghao Guo, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
2611.30310.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.

2611.30460.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
2611.30460.authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu
2611.30460.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

2611.30490.title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
2611.30490.authors: Puzhen Yuan, Yanjiang Guo, Yichen Liu, Xiang Zhu, Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Tun Ban, Haodong Yan, Zhide Zhong, Jianyu Chen
2611.30490.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.

2611.30534.title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
2611.30534.authors: Hyeonjae Kim, Jeongsol Kim, Sunwoo Park, Chanyu Moon, Yoojin Oh, Youngjun Jun, Kyumin Choi, Jong Chul Ye
2611.30534.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.

2611.30637.title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
2611.30637.authors: Hiroaki Honda, Koya Sakamoto, Shu Morikuni, Yusuke Iwasawa, Taiki Miyanishi
2611.30637.abstract: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench

2611.30658.title: Active Observation for Robust Visual Servoing in Robotic Manipulation
2611.30658.authors: Zhilun Hu, Yuqi Cheng, Yuxiang Tan, Wenpan Li, Weiming Shen
2611.30658.abstract: Robust visual servoing during robotic grasping remains challenging, as approach-phase occlusion frequently disrupts closed-loop control. To address this, we present an active observation framework in which one arm of an existing dual-arm platform carries an RGB-D camera as an active observer while the other executes grasping. The observer repositions to maintain or recover a shared target-gripper view within the feasible shared-view workspace. Occlusion during the final approach is particularly acute: fixed eye-to-hand lacks an active recovery mechanism once the target is hidden, while eye-in-hand can suffer from self-occlusion and sensitivity to hand-eye calibration. The observer first uses an active two-phase viewpoint strategy to align high-precision RGB-D axes with task-relevant error components. If visibility later degrades, an occlusion-triggered exploration module pauses the worker arm and scores candidate viewpoints by observation quality to recover a shared target-gripper view. Because both objects are detected in a single RGB-D image, the resulting Relative Servo Error avoids differencing two independently transformed target and gripper estimates. We evaluate the system on a dual 6-DoF Piper platform using an open-vocabulary detector with text prompts, without task-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations. Across 50 randomized trials per object, the system achieves 94% grasp success versus 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera. On triggered severe-occlusion trials, recovery takes $1.8 \pm 0.6$ s on average.

2611.30662.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
