Existing training-free methods attribute error accumulation to the loss of historical context and use attention sink to compensate for this loss. However, we find that visual degradation primarily stems from erroneous historical tokens, whose key-value pairs distort attention outputs. Although attention sink partially alleviates this issue, visual degradation persists. Motivated by the above analysis, we propose FreqForcing, a training-free framework that rectifies attention outputs in long-video generation via Spectral Self-Anchoring (SSA). The proposed SSA leverages the low-frequency components of anchor attention to maintain long-horizon visual stability, while preserving recent changes through the high-frequency components of local attention. FreqForcing extends models pretrained on 5s clips to minutes-long generation without finetuning. Extensive experiments show that FreqForcing outperforms existing training-free methods quantitatively and qualitatively.

2607.29278.title: Training-Free Entity-Level Few-Shot Segmentation of Remote Sensing Images with Advection Refinement
2607.29278.abstract: Existing cross-domain few-shot segmentation approaches suffer from high training costs due to source-domain episodic training and pixel-wise dense prediction, while often producing fragmented and noisy predictions in remote sensing images. To overcome these issues, we propose ELFSS-AR, a training-free entity-level few-shot segmentation method with advection refinement. Specifically, ELFSS-AR first leverages SAM3's generic geometric priors to generate category-agnostic entity primitives, and reformulates few-shot inference from pixel-level prediction to entity-level reasoning. Subsequently, foreground and background prototypes are constructed and combined with dense textual semantic responses from SAM3 to build a multi-modal semantic potential field. An advection equation-based semantic refinement mechanism is then introduced to propagate category-aware information across both feature and multi-source response spaces, further enhancing semantic continuity and suppressing local texture noise. Extensive experiments on multiple remote sensing datasets demonstrate that ELFSS-AR effectively mitigates domain shift and local noise, substantially improving SAM3's adaptation capability for remote sensing few-shot segmentation without additional training. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/yu-ni1989/ELFSS-AR.

2608.00066.title: PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable Remote Heart Rate Estimation
2608.00066.authors: Yehui Yang, Bo Zhao, Junzhe Cao, Hui Ma, Yue Sun, Wenjin Wang, Zitong Yu
2608.00066.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos, but its weak physiological signal is easily corrupted by motion, illumination changes, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. Existing rPPG methods typically rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, while different strong estimators may produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video. To resolve these conflicts, we propose PhysAgent, an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework. Unlike direct prediction approaches, PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to output heart rate directly. In contrast, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified and uses a lightweight 4B MLLM, Qwen3-VL-4B, to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate. Experimental results on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show that PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion. The code will be released soon.

2608.00076.title: Which Modality Decides? Counterfactual Modality Attribution for Multimodal Classifiers
2608.00076.authors: Vahidin Hasic, Chao Wang, Luis C. Garcia-Peraza-Herrera, David Watson, Senka Krivic
2608.00076.abstract: Multimodal classifiers can achieve high accuracy while exploiting modality-specific shortcuts. Modality attribution quantifies the contributions of image and text, but does not by itself identify which input changes would alter a suspicious prediction. We introduce Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), which connects modality-level contributions to explicit prediction-changing edits. CMA uses image and text diffusion priors to generate counterfactual references and constructs a two-player reference game whose Shapley--Taylor decomposition separates image, text, and interaction contributions. The method requires class-score queries but no model gradients. Attribution profiles are compared with a reference population to prioritize predictions with atypical modality reliance for review, while counterfactual edits expose localized evidence for inspection. On controlled image- and text-biased classifiers, CMA identifies the ground truth dominant modality for all evaluated inputs. On planted-shortcut benchmarks, it achieves shortcut-reliance detection AUROCs of 0.987 on Synthetic MNIST and 1.000 on OpenI, with image-shortcut localization IoUs of 0.97 and 0.84, respectively. An API experiment demonstrates applicability to a native multimodal language model with scored answer choices. CMA enables predictions to be screened by modality reliance and investigated through explicit counterfactual edits.

2608.01720.title: When Extreme Darkness Meets Motion Blur: MeanFlow for Unified RAW Restoration
2608.01720.authors: Zepu Wang, Jingze Liang, Weijie Xiao, Kexin Chen
2608.01720.abstract: Extremely low-light RAW enhancement aims to recover severely attenuated sensor signals, yet existing methods often focus on illumination and noise while overlooking the motion-induced degradations inherent in practical low-light imaging. We present a framework for robust extremely low-light RAW enhancement under realistic acquisition degradations. First, we introduce See in the Degraded Extremely Dark (SIDED), a new dataset that applies controlled motion degradation to extremely low-light RAW pairs while retaining their original sensor noise. Second, we propose a unified RAW tokenizer equipped with explicit domain-conditioned representation calibration to align extremely low-light and well-exposed RAW data, followed by a MeanFlow that performs enhancement in a single function evaluation. To our knowledge, this is the first work to formulate extremely low-light RAW enhancement under realistic motion-degraded acquisition and address it with MeanFlow. We further introduce a physics-guided refinement model to strengthen illumination--reflectance consistency, pixel fidelity, and color preservation without incurring additional inference cost. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in extremely low-light RAW enhancement, and robustly handles coupled motion and noise degradations.

2608.04701.title: UniWorld-View: Large-Baseline View Synthesis via Video Diffusion Models
2608.04701.authors: Wangbo Yu, Haiyang Zhou, Chaoran Feng, Xunyu Zhou, Li Yuan
2608.04701.abstract: Novel view synthesis from casually captured monocular images and videos offers a practical route to immersive content creation without dedicated multi-view capture. However, the limited viewpoint coverage of such inputs leaves scene geometry insufficiently constrained, restricting the ability of reconstruction-based methods, such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), to render views far from the observed viewpoints. Generative approaches leverage learned visual priors to synthesize unobserved content, but maintaining geometric consistency and precise camera control remains challenging under large viewpoint changes. We present UniView, a unified framework for large-baseline novel view synthesis and scene generation from monocular images and videos. Central to our approach are an occlusion-aware point cloud renderer and a dual-branch conditioning mechanism. The renderer uses triple reprojection to identify and filter unreliable projections under large viewpoint changes. The conditioning mechanism integrates the resulting geometric guidance with source-view appearance within the video diffusion model, enabling precise camera control while preserving visual details and synthesizing unobserved content. To extend view synthesis to scene generation, we introduce a two-stage generation strategy that decouples viewpoint changes from temporal evolution. This strategy produces dense, synchronized multi-view videos that provide additional supervision for dynamic Gaussian Splatting, enabling more complete 4D generation from monocular observations. Extensive evaluations across static and dynamic scenes demonstrate the effectiveness of UniView in novel view synthesis and scene generation, combining precise camera control with geometric consistency and visual fidelity.

2608.04935.title: Unleashing the Potential of Vision-Language Models for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
2608.04935.authors: Weihan Cai, Hao Tan, Zichang Tan, Jun Wan, Xinping Gao
2608.04935.abstract: A linear classifier trained on frozen DINOv3 features can outperform specialized detectors of AI-generated images in the wild. This success has motivated efforts to further adapt DINOv3 for detection, but we find that the same evaluation protocol underestimates the potential of a vision-language model. When linear probes are trained on images from the same generator, Perception Encoder (PE) performs worse than DINOv3 on in-the-wild benchmarks. Yet real and generated images form more distinct local groups in PE's frozen feature space. Image-text pretraining gives PE a source of supervision directly relevant to this distinction: captions can identify an image as AI-generated, allowing PE to learn high-level semantics about image provenance. Conventional linear probing uses only the image encoder. We introduce Semantic Prototype Calibration (SPC), which instead initializes the linear head of the frozen image encoder with text embeddings that describe real and AI-generated images. Across nine in-the-wild subsets, SPC raises mean accuracy from 84.8\% to 92.9\% for PE and from 81.4\% to 98.5\% for MoEViE. Both models also improve on controlled benchmarks. MoEViE-SPC outperforms specialized detectors with more elaborate task-specific designs. These results establish SPC as a simple and effective baseline for generalizable AI-generated image detection.

2608.16484.title: Remote-Sensing City Layout Extraction with MLLM
2608.16484.authors: Zigan Zhou, Kai Li, Yupeng Deng
2608.16484.abstract: Remote-sensing systems usually describe urban content with detection boxes, semantic masks, or vector boundaries. Such outputs locate classes and support image-plane scoring, yet they do not by themselves constitute an executable layout that retains object identities, typed relations, topology, and regeneration rules. Code-as-City instead casts urban-layout extraction from a single top-down image as constrained code generation with a multimodal large language model (MLLM). An image model first produces an aligned five-class semantic layout prior. Three ordered MLLM passes use the image and this prior to recover roads, land-cover regions and relations, and buildings. Deterministic normalization converts the accumulated records into a city graph and a restricted layout program. Executing the program creates a renderable 3D city layout and an orthographic semantic projection over shared geometry. The projection admits pixel-level comparison with remote-sensing masks, while named objects, relations, and editing operations remain available for synchronized regeneration of both views. Evaluated on the 100 scenes of CityLayout-100, the complete framework obtains 41.1% mean intersection-over-union and 48.3% global intersection-over-union. This result provides quantitative evidence that visual observations can be translated into inspectable, editable city code with coupled planar and 3D outputs.

2608.18339.title: From Inference to Adaptation: Vision-Language Model Test-Time Adaptation via a Unified Optimal Transport View
2608.18339.authors: Qi Yu, Zhichen Zeng, Katherine Tieu, Lingjie Chen, Xiyuan Yang, Ruizhong Qiu, Yuchen Yan, Lihui Liu, Yanjun Zhao, Ziao Wang, Lei Ying, Jingrui He, Hanghang Tong
2608.18339.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

2608.25344.title: CoRE: Weakly Supervised Coarse-to-Fine Risk Evidence Learning in Driving Videos
2608.25344.authors: Kaiser Hamid, Can Cui, Nade Liang
2608.25344.abstract: Driver perceived risk evolves in dynamic environments and is supported by specific scene entities, yet supervision is typically limited to coarse video-level judgments. Learning when supporting evidence emerges and which entities support a risk predictor would require costly temporal- and entity-level annotations. We introduce CoRE, a weakly supervised coarse-to-fine framework that learns fine-grained prediction support from coarse video supervision. CoRE trains and freezes a video-level predictor. Structured interventions over candidate temporal regions or entity tracks measure how each candidate changes the coarse prediction, producing graded prediction-effect targets. These targets are distilled into a student that directly predicts temporal and entity support from the original video, without interventions at inference. We evaluate this learning principle across three complementary settings. RISEE tests perceived-risk support from subjective clip-level judgments without temporal or entity-level risk annotations. DoTA provides independent temporal event annotations for evaluating weakly supervised traffic-anomaly localization. UCF-Crime tests whether the same coarse-to-fine mechanism extends to a standard non-driving anomaly-detection benchmark. Across these settings, CoRE learns informative fine-grained support from coarse supervision, with strong temporal localization on DoTA and competitive performance on UCF-Crime. These results establish coarse video predictions as supervision for recovering the fine-grained evidence supporting them, without corresponding fine-grained labels.

2608.25981.title: Race and gender differences in medical imaging models arise at the shared decision threshold
2608.25981.authors: Mahshad Lotfinia, Daniel Truhn, Andreas Maier, Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh
2608.25981.abstract: Fairness evaluations compare the performance of a medical imaging model between patient groups. A group difference in how well the model ranks images requires a better model, whereas a difference in error rates at the decision threshold shared by all groups can be addressed at the threshold. In studies of single chest radiograph models, race groups differed in error rates and hardly in ranking. However, to our knowledge, this has not been tested across image encoders, findings, and hospitals. We compared the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and false positive rate (FPR) between patient groups for 133 classification models from 13 public image encoders. The data comprised more than 700,000 images from 10 different public datasets of chest radiography, dermatology, and funduscopy. The tests resampled patients. Within each of the two hospitals with recorded race, no race difference in AUROC was statistically significant in any of the 117 chest radiograph models. By contrast, the race difference in FPR was significant in 107 models in one hospital, at a median of 12 more false positive calls per 100 radiographs without the finding, and in 54 models in the other, at a median of 6. The same held for 299 models from 22 encoders pretrained in this study with three objectives or race-balanced data and from a randomly initialized encoder. So within a hospital, the race groups differed significantly at the shared decision threshold and not in the ranking, whatever the encoder. Developers and hospitals could examine the decision threshold for each patient group before retraining a model to remove a group difference.

2608.28386.title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image
2608.28386.authors: Semin Kim, Haechan Shin, Jongyoo Kim
2608.28386.abstract: Existing monocular full-body 3D human-object interaction (HOI) methods do not combine category-agnostic object reconstruction with finger-level contact. Their hands may float off or sink into objects, breaking realism in AR/VR environments. We present GraspHOI, the first category-agnostic framework that reconstructs a full-body 3D HOI from a single image and jointly refines the arms and fingers so that the hands meet the reconstructed object surface. GraspHOI reconstructs the body, hands, and object separately with foundation models and places them in a shared metric camera frame through depth-based registration and silhouette alignment. Occlusion-aware contact correspondences seat the object against the hand, and contact-aware optimization refines shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger rotations while anchoring the joints to the image. We find that with fingers capped near the image estimate, refining them alone is insufficient; freeing the arm removes most of the remaining hand-object gap, since in a full body the arm chain places the hand. In experiments on three datasets, GraspHOI yields more plausible hand-object contact than four baselines and better relative human-object placement than HDM and TeHOR.

2608.28685.title: A Controlled, Internally Audited Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector
2608.28685.abstract: We test CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone for deepfake detection. Decision rules were frozen before the comparisons they govern were run; controls were matched on data, augmentation and, after an internal audit, training recipe; contrasts are paired on test videos. (1) Configuration result (registered STOP-gate, one seed): CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 -- as configured, not an architectural effect. (2) Recipe sensitivity: the control's recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); of changes reverted singly (one seed, descriptive), only the backbone learning rate's interval excluded zero, which replicated on two further seeds (exploratory; a sensitivity, not a causal decomposition). (3) Neutral result: at that baseline-derived recipe, the frequency-stream variants, not separately tuned, showed no detectable difference at the resolution of this experiment from the spatial control, under the evaluated configurations (post-audit pre-specified); a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 points at CRF 40 (exploratory). (4) One-configuration neutral result: the adversarial loss, restored at one strength, made no detectable difference (registered; 0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084). (5) Registered three-seed results: real H.264 outperforms JPEG at matched mean PSNR, by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec. These findings, and the advice to train on real compression levels, cover FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 data; diffusion content, transcoding chains and unknown codecs are untested.

2609.03429.title: When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits?
2609.03429.authors: Wonbin Son, Gyumun Choi, Junil Seo, Seungmin Rho, Mi Young Lee, Hyungjoon Kim
2609.03429.abstract: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a vision-language model (VLM) usually involves stating the assumption in text or editing the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is represented as a set of object tokens, and the model receives edited tokens without accompanying patch tokens from the original image. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to image-free object-token edits? We study this question in a simple testbed, keeping the visual encoder and language backbone frozen and training only a projector. Our analysis reveals three findings. Responsiveness depends on training: unlike standard VQA training, explicit edit training produces responsiveness in dense scenes and strengthens it in sparse scenes, across deletion, movement, and addition. Token construction and context token count shape responsiveness: the observed differences between token constructions appear to reflect more than token count alone, and responsiveness tends to weaken as surrounding context grows. Standard VQA performance and edit responsiveness are distinct: the object-token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-form VQA accuracy, and responses depend on the input tokens. The observed trends in responsiveness, token construction, and VQA retain their direction across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen language backbones. We release the evaluation-question generator, measurement records, scoring logs, and code.

2609.12181.title: Physics as the label for measuring and correcting materials reasoning in multimodal models
2609.12181.authors: Hasan Kurban, Rasul Khanbayov, Mustafa Kurban
2609.12181.abstract: Vision-language and language models increasingly interpret materials data, yet most benchmarks score final answers rather than whether the quantities a model states while reasoning obey established physical constraints. We introduce MatPCR, a label-free benchmark that uses six programmatic oracle families spanning diffraction geometry, microscopy scale, Raman peak structure, and Materials Project-grounded checks of near-hull stability, computed band-gap class, and net magnetization to test the physical admissibility of each checkable quantity a reasoning chain states, summarized as the Physical-Consistency Rate (PCR). The oracles are necessary-condition checks; their precision is audited by human review with interval estimates, and their recall on real responses is not assumed. Across nine models and 4,334 checkable records, overall PCR ranges from 0.556 to 0.778, and paired item-level tests separate only differences larger than about 0.07. Constraint-Grounded Self-Verification reduces oracle-detected violations in all four tested models; paired before-after scoring shows that it also raises answer correctness, but that most revisions which clear the oracle move to an admissible rather than an exact value. An open verifier reaches ROC AUC = 0.850 in distribution, varies strongly across constraint families, and does not transfer at a useful level to any held-out constraint family. An exact identity quantifies how oracle error displaces the reported PCR.

2609.14466.title: DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
2609.14466.authors: Calvin Galagain, Martyna Poreba, Fran\c{c}ois Goulette
2609.14466.abstract: Video segmentation models delineate and associate regions over time, but do not explicitly indicate whether they move independently of the camera. Query-based architectures propagate region representations across frames, raising a central question: can existing segmentation queries also support dynamicity prediction? We introduce DynEoMT, which adds a lightweight dynamicity head to existing segmentation queries without altering the segmentation or query-propagation architecture. To supervise this additional task, we generate class-agnostic pseudo-labels offline from camera-compensated optical flow. At inference, DynEoMT requires only the current frame and propagated queries, without explicit motion or geometric inputs. On VIPSeg, an MLP probe trained on frozen ViT-L queries achieves conditional balanced accuracy within 0.05 percentage points of full fine-tuning, suggesting that dynamicity-relevant information is already accessible in these representations. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, the ViT-B variant achieves conditional balanced accuracies of 84.30%, 67.98%, 68.59%, and 87.64%, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance with minimal overhead in the measured inference path.

2609.20066.title: PointEvent: Polarity-Conditioned Motion Evidence Accumulation for Event-Based Tiny Object Detection
2609.20066.authors: Zongze Wu, Baofeng Jia, Weiqi Yan, Jingyuan Zhang, Min Liu, Yu Zang, Xiaoyu Chen, Jing Han
2609.20066.abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets produce sparse, fragmented events easily overwhelmed by clutter and noise. Dense aggregation mixes weak target responses with background activity, while local spatiotemporal modeling may fail to connect distant observations. Polarity encodes the sign of brightness change; a moving target tends to produce opposite polarities at its leading and trailing boundaries, whose spatial arrangement indicates motion direction. We propose PointEvent, which serializes events into complementary spatiotemporal and timestamp orders. Spatiotemporal orders preserve x-y-t locality, while timestamp orders preserve temporal succession across spatial neighborhoods, establishing long-range propagation paths. Along each path, a recurrent state accumulates evidence, while polarity routes each event to its corresponding state subspace. This separates how evidence propagates from where it is written. Experiments on EV-UAV and ES-UAV demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with the fewest parameters (0.12M) and fastest measured inference (29.9 ms) among compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

2609.24984.title: WorldCrafter: Consistent Video World Model with Implicit 3D-aware Memory
2609.24984.authors: Wangbo Yu, Kunhao Liu, Wenbo Hu, Shenghai Yuan, Chaoran Feng, Haiyang Zhou, Yukun Huang, Yiran Wang, Wang Zhao, Yingmin Luo, Ying Shan
2609.24984.abstract: Video world models enable interactive exploration of dynamic environments, yet struggle to respect prior observations over long horizons and across viewpoints. We present WorldCrafter, a video world model that learns a camera-queryable implicit 3D-aware memory for this purpose. The key insight is to let the requested viewpoint shape how multi-view evidence is compressed into the video generator's limited token budget. Trained jointly with the video generator, a memory encoder and pose-conditioned readout module integrate historical observations into a fixed set of target view-specific tokens before denoising, without explicit depth-based correspondences. By combining this memory with recent temporal context and few-step distillation, WorldCrafter enables streaming scene exploration from a single input image or text prompt. Experiments across static and dynamic scenes show substantial gains in long-horizon consistency and camera-control accuracy while preserving visual quality during minute-scale exploration.

2609.32537.title: RIPE-MambaSpike: Resolution-Independent Spiking-State-Space Interfaces for Parameter-Efficient Event-Based Vision
2609.32537.authors: Md Muhiminul Islam, Shoaib Ahmed Dipu, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
2609.32537.abstract: Spiking-Mamba hybrids reach strong accuracy on event-based vision, but existing designs often require tens of millions of parameters. In hybrids that flatten the spiking feature map and project it densely into the scan, much of that cost comes from this interface rather than from the hybrid architecture itself. In a representative model, a single resolution-dependent projection accounts for 33.55M of 36.25M parameters. To that end, we introduce RIPE-MambaSpike (Resolution-Independent, Parameter-Efficient), which replaces that projection with a hierarchical multi-resolution bridge of fixed channel width. Its deployed footprint is 0.870M parameters, constant at fixed time steps and widths across a 43x range of input areas. Reparameterized spiking stages, temporal decoupled modulation, and a dynamic convex-hull-bounded dual-stream membrane-potential attention preserve accuracy under this compact design. Result-wise, RIPE-MambaSpike is pareto-optimal on CIFAR10-DVS, N-Caltech101, and DailyDVS-200. Notably, on the 200-class DailyDVS-200, a scaled 8.04M configuration achieves 45.7% top-1 accuracy, the best reported spiking result on that benchmark, and outperforms prior spiking methods with 3.0-15.1x fewer parameters than dense ANNs. Overall, our findings demonstrate that competitive event-based recognition does not require resolution-dependent parameter growth. Code is available at https://github.com/MuhiminOsim/RIPE-MambaSpike.

2609.34047.title: ARCH-B: Architectural Representation, Comprehension and Hierarchy Benchmark
2609.34047.authors: Kieran Sagar Parikh, Jose Luis Garcia del Castillo y Lopez
2609.34047.abstract: Multimodal models increasingly interpret visual environments, but their ability to recognize the same building across photographs, floor plans, elevations, sections, and renderings remains poorly characterized. We introduce ARCH-B, a benchmark of 354 four-choice questions across 11 cross-representational archetypes, constructed from a building-linked corpus of 3.9 million architectural images using visually similar distractors, model-guided difficulty screening, and manual validation. We evaluate 25 multimodal models and collect 5,830 responses from non-expert human participants. Model accuracy ranges from 10.45% to 83.90%, compared with a human baseline of 35.35%. Models perform comparatively well on mixed-representation outlier detection and photograph matching, but remain weaker on floorplan-to-photograph correspondence. Human and model difficulty across archetypes is only weakly correlated (Spearman's (\rho=0.33)). Held-out evaluation confirms that the difficulty identified during screening generalizes beyond the curation models. ARCH-B provides a diagnostic evaluation of visual correspondence and representation transfer across architectural media.

2609.34237.title: DecFlowEdit: Self-Localized Flow-based Image Editing via Guidance Decoupling
2609.34237.authors: Zheyuan Zhan, Can Wang, Jiawei Chen, Chun Chen, Siwei Lyu, Zeyu Zheng, Defang Chen
2609.34237.abstract: Flow-based image editing (FlowEdit) enables inversion-free semantic changes through the difference between source and target velocities. In this paper, we observe that FlowEdit's default classifier-free guidance (CFG) configuration, with asymmetric source and target scales, causes substantial background leakage. Matching these guidance scales, for example by removing CFG, improves edit-relevant localization but severely degrades editability. To get the best of both worlds, we propose DecFlowEdit, which decouples the optimal guidance scales for localization and for editing in flow-based generative models. In particular, DecFlowEdit first extracts an edit-relevant prior by temporally aggregating velocity differences evaluated without CFG, and then uses this prior to reweight the original updates under default CFG. Our method remains training-free and inversion-free, requiring neither external spatial masks nor attention manipulation. Experiments on PIE-Bench across FLUX.1-dev, SD3, and SD3.5 show that DecFlowEdit improves background preservation, reducing structure distance by approximately 61-73% and background LPIPS by 68-80% relative to FlowEdit at comparable editing fidelity.

2609.34630.title: Long Time No See: Benchmarking VLMs for Out-of-Sight Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Egocentric Videos
2609.34630.authors: Fangzhou Ma, Ivo Alexander Ban, Eren Homburg, Gabriele Goletto, R\'emi Pautrat, Mahdi Rad, Chiara Plizzari, Marc Pollefeys
2609.34630.abstract: Real-world AI systems must reason about objects that are no longer visible: an AR assistant guiding a user back to an object used earlier, a household robot retrieving an item someone put away. This requires not just recalling where an object was last seen, but updating its state when it is moved and retaining that update once it leaves view. We refer to this as out-of-sight spatiotemporal reasoning. We introduce Beyond3D, the first VQA benchmark to isolate this ability in dynamic egocentric video: every query targets an object that has been relocated and has since left the field of view. We create our questions from HD-EPIC annotations, building a visibility track for each dynamic object from its 3D position, the camera pose, and the scene geometry to understand at each moment whether it is visible, occluded, or out of view. Beyond3D comprises 9,000 questions in eight types over 135 videos from nine participants, organized as one reasoning chain: visual grounding (is the target observable now), temporal grounding (when it was last visible and last placed), scene localization (which fixture anchors that location), and 3D spatial perception (where it lies relative to the current viewpoint or another object in the scene). We benchmark nine general-purpose and spatially specialized VLMs. The best model reaches 42.2% against 29.7% chance and text-only baselines reaching 31.9%, with the largest failures in recovering when an object was last visible, showing that tracking object movement out of sight remains far from solved for current VLMs.

2609.36217.title: Sparse-View Interpretable 3D Animal Behavior Representations for Neural Encoding and Decoding
2609.36217.authors: Xinming Dai, Qihang Jin, Tianshu Tan, Baiyuan Chen, Hanrui Lyu, Lenny Aharon, Kyle Daruwalla, Xun Helen Hou, Matthew R. Whiteway, Liam Paninski, Yizi Zhang
2609.36217.abstract: A deeper understanding of brain function requires a precise, structured characterization of behavior. Yet, extracting behavioral representations from video in a form suitable for scientific analysis remains a fundamental challenge. Many prior studies represent behavior via pose estimation or nonlinear video embeddings. However, pose tracking discards rich information beyond predefined keypoints, while nonlinear video embeddings lack interpretability. We address this limitation with SABLE (Sparse-view Animal Behavior Latent Embeddings), a self-supervised framework that leverages a geometric inductive bias to learn behavior representations. By augmenting a multi-view transformer with priors from monocular depth and pose estimation, SABLE reconstructs 3D animal behavior from extremely sparse views while learning explicit 3D latent structure. Without ground-truth 3D labels, it reliably recovers 3D behavior from two-view videos, whereas state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods fail or yield degenerate solutions. Across the International Brain Lab and Cheese3D datasets, we demonstrate that SABLE learns 3D representations that match or exceed prior SOTA performance in neural encoding and decoding. Single-neuron analyses further identify neurons with putative 3D tuning, generating testable hypotheses about how the brain represents 3D behavior. Once pretrained across animals, SABLE serves as an off-the-shelf model that generalizes zero-shot to unseen animals without animal-specific calibration or retraining. Our method establishes 3D-aware video embeddings that capture complex behavior, opening new avenues for studying brain-behavior relationships.

2610.01013.title: SparSelect: Training-Free Sparse Attention for Efficient 3D Reconstruction
2610.01013.authors: Junyi Wu, Fanqing Kong, Leyang Chen, Shaoqiu Zhang, Yulun Zhang
2610.01013.abstract: Feed-forward 3D vision models such as VGGT have achieved remarkable progress, unifying camera estimation and dense scene reconstruction in a single pass. However, their quadratic global attention makes long image sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may favor highly attended yet value-redundant regions. To address these limitations, we introduce SparSelect, a training-free sparse attention method combining value-aware block selection and key-guided prioritization. Our value-aware block selection integrates pooled query-key relevance with value contrast to select high-priority blocks, reducing redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content. Key-guided prioritization further refines block selection by grouping similar keys and prioritizing key features underrepresented in the initial selection. Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D demonstrate improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, together with up to $2.27\times$ faster inference than dense VGGT. Code and evaluation scripts will be made available.

2610.05066.title: Salvation Lies Within: Eliciting Inherent Style Transfer in Step-Distilled Diffusion Models
2610.05066.authors: Shengyin Sun, Yiming Li, Yingzhao Lian, Xing Li, Xingzhi Zhou, Anxin Tian, Zhili Wang, Haoyang Li, Ziqiang Cui, Chen Ma
2610.05066.abstract: Adapting step-distilled text-to-image (T2I) models through post-training incurs additional computational costs and affects native few-step generation behavior. This motivates a complementary route beyond style-specific adaptation: drawing on the visual knowledge already encoded in step-distilled T2I models to elicit stylistic capabilities through language. Pursuing this direction requires textual guidance that captures how visual attributes jointly define a style and remain applicable as the depicted content changes. To explore this approach, we introduce StyleForge, a fully automatic, training-free framework that expresses reference styles as reusable rendering instructions. By integrating overall rendering characteristics with local color and lighting behavior, StyleForge organizes visual evidence from reference images into a coherent specification of how the target style should be expressed. The specification is then compiled into textual guidance that can be reused across content prompts, enabling frozen step-distilled T2I models to render different subjects and scenes in the reference style while retaining native few-step generation. Extensive experiments show relative gains of up to 29.47\% in generation quality scores over the strongest baseline, while Pareto analysis indicates that improved stylization is accompanied by strong adherence to the requested content. Code is available at https://github.com/sunshy-1/StyleForge.

2610.07705.title: What Frame-Level Labels Can and Cannot Do for Small-UAV Point Detection in Thermal Video
2610.07705.authors: Wonbin Son, Gyumum Choi, Junil Seo, Hyungjoon Kim
2610.07705.abstract: The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has increased the importance of image-based UAV detection. Learning-based detectors are trained on imagery and annotations, with annotation type determining the information available during training. We focus on learning localization from frame-level target presence/absence labels when sensor or scene changes make spatial annotations for additional training burdensome. We analyze the detection capability, learning behavior, and potential applications of an existing architecture for point detection of small UAVs, trained with presence/absence labels and requiring no external detector. The architecture freezes spatial features learned through classification and trains a readout with the same frame labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. On two thermal infrared datasets, CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410, we evaluate localization hit rates and detection rates under false-alarm constraints, analyze the effects of training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration, and compare with bounding-box detectors. We also explore potential applications on Airborne Object Tracking (AOT) using its visible-light imagery and frame labels. Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses, while readout training helped extract them consistently. Distributing similar label counts across more videos yielded higher localization hit rates, while synthesis effects varied by dataset and evaluation criterion. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints, and failures remained when target signals were weak relative to background variation and under cross-dataset transfer. These findings provide guidance on label allocation, spatial representations and readouts, synthesis, and false-alarm control.

2610.10181.title: Argos: Adapt Rich Geometric Priors for Generalizable Online Scene-Change-Detection
2610.10181.authors: Ruihan Xu, Jiae Yoon, Kaichen Zhou, Ue-Hwan Kim, Luca Carlone
2610.10181.abstract: Robots operating in dynamic environments require reliable detection of how their surroundings change over time. Existing learning-based methods largely rely on pairwise 2D image features, which struggle under large viewpoint changes and occlusions, are sensitive to noise, and show limited generalization across domains, while explicit 3D approaches typically require costly offline optimization. We show that the implicit 3D knowledge of Geometric Foundation Models (GFMs) provides a strong basis for addressing these limitations. We introduce Argos, which adapts GFM features for joint scene change detection and 3D reconstruction. To address data scarcity and take a step toward a foundation model for scene change detection, we introduce a large-scale benchmark comprising two synthetic datasets and one real-world dataset, and train jointly across diverse datasets to improve cross-domain generalization. We further introduce Argos-SLAM, a real-time system designed for robotics, which performs online change detection and change-aware 4D mapping. Across benchmarks, our framework substantially outperforms existing baselines, with gains of up to 42.01% in change IoU and 27.91% in F1, while supporting scalable deployment in changing real-world environments.

2610.10703.title: Seeing Through the Glare: A Multi-Source Benchmark and Ocular-Adaptive Pixel MeanFlow for Eyeglass Reflection Removal
2610.10703.authors: Tao Liu, Youwei Pang, Kailai Zhou, Jiaming Zuo, Hanqi Liu, Wei Ji, Peng-Tao Jiang, Xiaofeng Liu, Weisi Lin, Xiaoqi Zhao
2610.10703.abstract: Eyeglass reflection removal is important across smartphone imaging, video conferencing, and other face-centric visual applications. The task is challenging because reflections range from mild photometric contamination to severe ocular occlusion, requiring selective correction and plausible reconstruction without altering identity or natural appearance. Existing datasets cover limited reflection conditions, constraining generalization to complex real-world scenes and systematic evaluation. We introduce OcuBench, a multi-source benchmark comprising 10,280 controllable synthetic pairs, 732 real-input pseudo-pairs, and 458 independent real-world test images, supporting both paired evaluation and assessment beyond generated supervision. We further propose OcuFlow, an ocular-adaptive pixel MeanFlow (pMF) framework for efficient, detail-preserving restoration. It combines geometry-adaptive representation with one-step pMF to focus reconstruction on reflection-obscured ocular regions, together with native-resolution frequency-preserving synthesis to retain reliable observed details. Experiments across diverse reflection conditions demonstrate that OcuFlow achieves consistent advantages in reflection removal quality, ocular fidelity, and efficiency. In a blind user study, it receives $67.32\%$ of selections, $6.2\times$ the next-best share. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/NTU-AI4X/OcuFlow.

2610.11058.title: Refine Connections, Close the Gap: A Reliable Enhancement Framework for Driving Scene Topology
2610.11058.authors: Xiaoqi Wang, Dingyi Zhuang, David Paz, Wenbin He, Yucai Bai, Peng Zhou, Rui Zhang, Jinhua Zhao, Liu Ren
2610.11058.abstract: In autonomous driving, understanding scene topology -- the connectivity between lanes and traffic elements -- is critical for safe path planning and motion control. While current methods excel at detecting individual map elements, their connectivity reasoning often falls short of its theoretical potential, leaving a significant performance gap relative to the theoretical upper-bound (Oracle) achievable given the underlying detections. To bridge this gap, we propose TopoEnhance, a novel topology enhancement framework designed to unlock the latent potential of existing methods by refining their connectivity predictions. We formulate topology enhancement as a denoising-based reconstruction process, where the model learns to recover structural consistency from stochastically corrupted ground-truth graphs. This training strategy does not require predictions from upstream topology models. Experiments on OpenLane-V2 show that TopoEnhance consistently improves $TOP_{ll}$ and $TOP_{lt}$ across diverse prediction sources, narrowing the gap to the detection-conditioned Upper-Bound without source-specific retraining. Further evaluations demonstrate improvements in ego-route recoverability, downstream trajectory prediction, and temporal consistency.

2610.12978.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
2610.12978.authors: Zihao Pan, Mengting Chen, Cheng Shi, Taihang Hu, Zhengrong Yue, Zikang Wang, Yuan Wang, Wei Li, Sibei Yang
2610.12978.abstract: Visual representations are largely developed for understanding, yet what makes them useful for generation remains unclear. We study this question in pixel diffusion transformers and uncover two key insights. First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility, as externally aligned semantics can be progressively lost during pixel synthesis. Second, architectural separation with specialized pixel decoders mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling, without necessarily yielding representations better suited to generation. These insights suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited. Motivated by these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG), which directly forms and exploits internal representations while retaining a plain Transformer architecture. A low-dimensional bottleneck forces generation-relevant information into a compact representation, which is then explicitly used to guide decoder generation by modifying the flow-matching target according to its induced prediction offset. RG learns clearer semantic and spatial structure while scaling efficiently in both parameters and computation. On ImageNet 256x256, RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters outperforms substantially larger pixel diffusion transformers, while RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55. RG further reaches an FID of 1.74 at 512x512 and extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.89 on GenEval and 87.1 on DPG-Bench.

2610.13259.title: Beyond a Single Crop: In-Context Adaptation for Player Re-Identification
2610.13259.authors: Ge Luo, Changhuo Yang, Weisi Fan, Rui Yang, Shaokai Wang
2610.13259.abstract: Person re-identification is typically addressed by learning identity-discriminative embeddings from individual person crops. However, player re-identification in broadcast sports videos presents a unique challenge: players from the same team often share similar appearances. Conventional methods encode each player crop independently, overlooking the surrounding players and repeated observations that could help resolve these ambiguities. Here, we propose ContextReID, a framework for visual in-context adaptation that represents a player by jointly considering other players in the same frame and observations from different frames of the broadcast sequence. We implement this framework with a vision-language backbone trained with contrastive objectives for player retrieval and identity matching across the supplied context. Without requiring parameter updates or context identity labels at inference, the trained model adapts the target embedding to the supplied visual context. Experiments on SportsMOT, DanceTrack, and SoccerNet-GSR demonstrate superior retrieval performance compared with single-crop baselines. Cross-sport transfer experiments within SportsMOT further show that in-context adaptation can improve retrieval on sports excluded from training. These results highlight the empirical value of our method in utilizing spatial and temporal context without requiring identity labels or cross-frame identity associations at inference.

2610.20556.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
2610.20556.authors: Yubo Huang, Yuxuan Zhang, Weiqiang Wang, Jiaming Liu, Sirui Zhao, Enhong Chen
2610.20556.abstract: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted suffix remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk generation. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and generation time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

2610.21302.title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
2610.21302.authors: Minhyeok Roh, Minseo Lee, Jun Young Jeong, Byeonghyeon Lee, Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Jaesik Park, Eunbyung Park
2610.21302.abstract: Dynamic Gaussian representations enable high-quality, real-time volumetric video, with FreeTimeGS standing out as a high-performing approach. Nevertheless, challenging motion remains a persistent issue in dynamic Gaussian reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that these failures stem not from limited representational capacity alone, but also from where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. To address these limitations, we augment FreeTimeGS with two Gaussian allocation strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, then reinitializes low-opacity Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations inferred from multi-view observations, independently of their previous locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying FreeTimeGS representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly for small, rapidly moving objects and fine appearance details in highly dynamic regions.

2610.23600.title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
2610.23600.authors: Mengtan Zhang, Yuchuan Cui, Yu Ma, Zizhan Guo, Wei Ye, Rui Fan
2610.23600.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.

2610.26915.title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
2610.26915.authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu, Liwei Bao
2610.26915.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) recognizes ongoing actions in streaming video, often relying on RGB appearance and optical flow. Codec motion vectors (MVs) provide motion information at low computational cost, but directly replacing Flow with MVs can reduce detection accuracy. Our analysis shows that Flow and MVs capture similar dominant motion patterns; fine-grained motion details contribute less after RGB fusion, but motion still provides complementary cues that RGB alone cannot fully capture, helping maintain detection accuracy. The remaining gap between RGB+Flow and RGB+MV narrows substantially for conditional category identity but persists for action presence, where motion-only predictions provide complementary evidence. We propose CodecMotion-OAD to replace Flow with MVs in existing two-stream detectors. To our knowledge, this is the first use of codec MVs as a Flow substitute in frame-level causal OAD. Its unlabeled motion representation adaptation initializes an MV encoder with Flow-pretrained weights and adapts it through feature alignment. It also employs presence-identity routing to improve action presence estimation using complementary motion-only evidence while preserving the joint detector's conditional category distribution. On IPPP-re-encoded THUMOS'14, CodecMotion-OAD with MiniROAD achieves 69.60 mAP versus 70.39 for RGB+Flow, with 1.99-fold GPU and 11.13-fold CPU decoder-to-prediction speedups.

2610.28087.title: WildAIGC-Bench: Can AI Image Detectors Handle the Wild?
2610.28087.authors: Zijian Yu, Hangwei Zhang, Shunxing Chen, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Jianfu Zhang
2610.28087.abstract: An AI-generated scene or a subtle edit to a photograph can make a false claim about a public event appear credible. Existing benchmarks test detectors across generators and platforms, but offer limited insight into how well they recognize fabrications that circulate as evidence for such claims. We introduce WildAIGC-Bench, an event-driven benchmark designed for broad coverage, timely updates, and human-verified labels. A recurring search across news outlets, fact-checking sites, and social posts identifies emerging cases, and reviewers verify the evidence for each image. The benchmark contains 600 AI-generated or edited images and 638 genuine photographs of related subjects. It preserves posts alongside crops of the depicted images and links documented edits to their original photographs where available. All ten visual detectors achieve lower balanced accuracy on WildAIGC-Bench than their respective averages across eight external benchmarks with both classes. On 37\% of the AI images, at least three quarters of the evaluated detectors predict real. Cropping improves recall for most visual detectors but reduces it for most general-purpose multimodal models. Comparisons with editing originals further reveal local alterations that most detectors miss even when they correctly accept the original photograph.

2610.28339.title: HistoLoop: Coarse-to-Fine Spatial Context Integration with a Looped Transformer for Histology-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
2610.28339.authors: Ziang Liu, Jie Liu, Shuai Li, Yigui Feng, Qinglin Wang
2610.28339.abstract: Inferring spatial gene expression from routine H&E slides requires interpreting local morphology within a tissue organization that spans multiple spatial scales. Existing multi-scale methods, however, compute regional summaries at each scale only once and then combine them across scales, rather than forming finer-scale summaries from representations that have already absorbed coarser-scale context. We propose HistoLoop, a looped Transformer that integrates spatial context progressively from coarse to fine. HistoLoop applies a shared set of modules across recurrent steps at increasingly fine resolutions, and constructs the context at each step from spot states that have already absorbed coarser-scale context. On HEST-1k, a single model trained jointly on six cancer types achieves a macro-averaged HVG50 Pearson correlation of 0.480, compared with 0.435 for the strongest baseline. Ablations show that the multi-resolution loop, the coarse-to-fine schedule, and the dependence of each step on updated spot states each contribute to this performance, and clustering analysis indicates that HistoLoop better preserves the multigene structure of tissue domains. On cancer types held out from training, HistoLoop attains the highest average correlation, although transfer to unseen cancer types remains challenging for all methods.

2610.33965.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: An Efficiency- and Statistics-Aware Benchmark of ResNet50 and Vision Transformer for Explainable Multi-Class Gastrointestinal Diseases Classification
2610.33965.abstract: Automated classification of gastrointestinal (GI) findings in endoscopic images could support early diagnosis, but architectures are often chosen on accuracy alone. We present a controlled, reproducible benchmark of ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 for eight-class GI classification on the public Kvasir dataset (4,000 images), using a stratified split (400 test images) and stratified group 5-fold cross-validation over all images. In cross-validation, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 reached 92.12% and 91.70% accuracy, and a two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure showed equivalence within a +/-3 percentage-point margin (difference +0.43 points, 90% CI -0.33 to +1.18; p < 0.001). The architectures differed mainly in cost: ResNet50 had 3.6 times fewer parameters and 4.3 times fewer operations, 2.5-fold lower single-image CPU latency (69 vs. 177 ms) and 3.8-fold higher GPU throughput. Cross-validated calibration was similar (expected calibration error 0.021 vs. 0.023). An edge-oriented transformer, MobileViT-S, was most accurate on the test split (95.5%) but lost 9.4 points when an acquisition artefact present in some classes (the ScopeGuide inset) was occluded, whereas ResNet50 was not significantly affected. On 500 unseen polyp images with expert masks, both models' Grad-CAM maps focused on the lesion (3.6 times chance). On a de-duplicated external subset of GastroVision (1,998 images), accuracy fell to 78-80% for all three models and differences between them remained small. Accuracy differences between architectures were thus small relative to the effects of shortcut learning and domain shift, whereas efficiency differences were large. An efficient CNN is a defensible default for resource-constrained screening, but no model is deployment-ready without local validation.

2610.35904.title: ObjectTwin: Training-Free Asset Verification for Captured Scenes
2610.35904.abstract: An editable digital twin needs assets that faithfully represent the particular objects captured. Partial observations leave both unseen geometry and asset placement uncertain: several registrations can explain the available views while predicting different surfaces elsewhere. We introduce ObjectTwin, a training-free framework for capture-conditioned asset verification. It retains calibration-compatible alignments, checks observed surfaces and known free space, and carries the resulting range of evidence into acceptance, exclusion, or deferred inspection. Withheld observations evaluate each fixed decision. Across Replica and ScanNet, capture correspondence improves held-out asset selection over registered geometry, reducing mean IoU regret by 55% on shared candidate pairs. Across multiview reconstruction, amodal completion, and scene generation, surface-based selection identifies the best unseen-view candidate for 97.5% of shared test objects. Controlled edits verify sensitivity to visible errors and invariance to unobserved geometry. Compatible alignments also predict different unseen outcomes, while strong single-fit controls distinguish this sensitivity from gains in screening accuracy. Together, these experiments establish capture correspondence as a useful asset-selection signal and provide a reproducible framework for evaluating absolute quality and alignment-dependent decisions.

2610.36853.title: D4GS: Efficient Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Depth Priors
2610.36853.authors: Da Li, Yihan Zang, Ivan Viola, Zeyu Wang, Dominik Engel
2610.36853.abstract: Achieving high-quality reconstruction and responsive camera tracking remains challenging for monocular RGB Gaussian splatting SLAM under a limited optimization budget. We present an online system that addresses this challenge by combining learned geometric priors with explicit geometric camera tracking, which efficiently performs camera tracking while maintaining the map to keep the predicted depth scale consistent. A frozen depth model serves as a virtual RGB-D sensor, providing depth estimation from monocular video. An explicit geometric solver then estimates camera pose through feature reprojection, and a streaming Gaussian mapper integrates the resulting observations into a dense scene representation. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets show that our method significantly improves reconstruction quality over existing approaches, achieving over 10 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and delivering almost twice the throughput of the evaluated fastest prior SLAM systems on the 7-Scenes dataset.

2610.37036.title: GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing
2610.37036.abstract: We present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into 2D and 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) indoor scenes, accounting for lighting interactions between objects and their surroundings. We lift albedo, roughness, metallic and normals from diffusion-based 2D priors onto the Gaussians by back-projection, model windows and lamps as analytic area emitters, and recover their absolute radiance from ordinary LDR captures with a low-dimensional fit over unit-radiance bases. A path tracer over Gaussians and meshes then produces view-consistent shading, interreflections and soft shadows, which are composited onto the original reconstruction by differential rendering, preserving the untouched background. On synthetic, real and generated scenes, GraftRay outperforms recent insertion and inverse-rendering baselines in image fidelity and shadow accuracy at competitive cost, and users prefer its lighting and shadows over those of the baselines.

2610.37503.title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping
2610.37503.authors: Ivan Shchekotov, Timofei Gritsaev, Viacheslav Pirogov, Dmitry Vetrov
2610.37503.abstract: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training samples.

2610.38360.title: SparseTokenGS: Gaussian-based Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction via Reusable Token Pool
2610.38360.authors: Zihan Deng, Zhenzhen Gong, Yujie Liu, Jiaxin Gong, Dingkun Liu, Kexian Xie, Yixing Huang, Peng Jin, Tianye Niu, Zhisheng Wang, Fenglin Liu, Hongming Shan, Lequan Yu
2610.38360.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography is widely used for fast, low-dose volumetric imaging and lesion localization in dentistry and image-guided interventions, but it introduces severe artifacts. Feed-forward Gaussian methods transfer the reconstruction cost to training and decode each coordinate from projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. However, information from the whole scan is written only when the field is constructed and cannot be retrieved during coordinate decoding, leaving the volume inconsistent within the scan. This is a common limitation of such methods: once the field is fixed, decoding uses only local features and reconstruction quality drops substantially. We propose SparseTokenGS, a Gaussian-based method for sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography reconstruction via a reusable token pool. Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention query this shared pool at the anchors and at the query coordinates, respectively. The local Gaussian prior is retained, and the volume is reconstructed in one forward pass, without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. On three public chest and dental datasets, SparseTokenGS achieves the highest reconstruction performance among the compared methods. On clinical dental scans, reconstruction from only six projections reaches 29.51 decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio and a structural similarity of 0.842 against the full-view reference, and off-the-shelf tooth-and-pulp segmentation keeps these structures separable for root-canal localization. Experiments on volcanic rock and chicken show performance after same-object adaptation. A reusable token pool gives feed-forward reconstruction a mechanism that keeps scan-wide context available through decoding and can benefit future rapid clinical lesion localization and analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/FrankDengAI/SparseTokenGS.

2610.40935.title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
2610.40935.authors: Zeping Zhang, Zhuoya Zhao, Robert Lagani\`ere
2610.40935.abstract: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$. Each kept token receives a 3D anchor from its LiDAR point and is fed to a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future features and 3D displacements without box annotations. At 25% budget, GATS achieves a 3-sec L2 displacement error of 0.520 m on nuScenes and an EPDMS of 88.9 on NAVSIM---surpassing the dense baseline (0.573 m / 85.9) at $6.6\times$ fewer total FLOPs. At an extreme 10% budget (24 GFLOPs, $18\times$ reduction), it still beats the dense baseline on both nuScenes (0.537 m vs. 0.573 m L2) and NAVSIM (87.9 vs. 85.9 EPDMS). On 739 intent-critical scenarios, GATS covers 95.8% of hazardous vehicles and achieves a 0.09% collision rate---73.5% lower than the dense model (0.34%).

2610.41231.title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
2610.41231.authors: Gaige Wang, Bowen Pan, Hao Ren, Jiangjing Lyu, Chengfei Lyu
2610.41231.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

2610.41373.title: Queryable Gaussian View Index: Retrieval, Localization, and Agentic View Search
2610.41373.authors: Tianyu Xiong, Rui Li, Jiaqi Yang
2610.41373.abstract: Given an existing 3D Gaussian scene and calibrated references, we seek camera poses and views that answer text, RGB, or image-and-instruction queries. RGB localization recovers a source camera; a target-view instruction can require a different camera while preserving the referenced scene content. Queryable Gaussian View Index (QGVI) supports these requests through a semantic view index that binds structured captions and observations to calibrated camera poses. QGVI-T retrieves indexed candidates with BM25. QGVI-A uses this interface and geometric source localization (QGVI-I) as tools, sharing candidate poses, observations, and query conditions marked satisfied, violated, or unknown. Unmet conditions guide camera proposals and rendered checks. Supported answers exit early; unresolved queries return insufficient evidence within a shared search budget. We construct a nine-scene benchmark, including city-scale environments, covering semantic view retrieval, RGB localization with out-of-map rejection, and image-conditioned target-view search. Under GPT assessment on the development cohort, QGVI-A returns confirmed correct views for 90.4\% of target-view queries, compared with 26.8\% for one-shot Retrieve + Select. This comparison evaluates complete policies with different information and call budgets; QGVI-A achieves higher coverage at lower answer precision. The benchmark separates semantic satisfaction, source-camera accuracy, and acceptance decisions.

2610.41790.title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation
2610.41790.authors: Eunseob Choi, Kyeonghun Kim, Hyuk-Jae Lee, Nam-Joon Kim
2610.41790.abstract: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.

2611.00804.title: Training-free Conditional Object Composition for Multi-object Image Generation with Diffusion Models
2611.00804.abstract: Multi-object image generation in text-to-image diffusion models remains challenging, as existing approaches struggle to reliably generate all objects specified in a prompt. Compositional approaches that generate objects independently often fail to capture the interactions among them, whereas joint generation methods tend to suffer from inter-object interference. In this work, we propose a training-free framework, termed conditional object composition, that relaxes joint generation methods by taking one step back toward compositional approaches. Our framework decomposes the generation of $N$ objects into two stages: it first generates a subset of $N-1$ objects and then composes the remaining object conditioned on the generated content. To enable effective composition, we adopt an inpainting-based formulation with layout guidance to preserve existing regions and encourage spatially coherent placement. To address the challenge of selecting which objects to generate separately, we introduce an attention-based scoring mechanism based on cross-attention maps and further explore the use of off-the-shelf object detectors. We evaluate our method on multi-object image generation using the widely adopted MS COCO dataset. Experimental results show that our approach achieves competitive or improved performance compared to existing methods, particularly as the number of objects increases. Further studies highlight the importance of the proposed design choices. The source code is available at https://github.com/ShampooWang/condComp_imageGen/tree/main

2611.00937.title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
2611.00937.authors: Yubin Jing, Ziyang Zhang, Meng Chen, Yuyao Li, Haofan Wang, Yichen Gong
2611.00937.abstract: Autoregressive video generators produce videos block by block from historical context. They are trained within a bounded horizon, whereas inference can extend far beyond it, causing temporal consistency to gradually decrease. Existing methods focus on eliminating this mismatch, but we instead ask whether the historical context used in training remains suitable for inference. Each block reads historical context in two stages, when denoising generates it and when committing writes it into the KV cache for later blocks. We find that older historical context such as the sink helps denoising but can hurt later blocks when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. We also show that as committing reads more preceding blocks, clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. We therefore propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. Each committing pass reads only the preceding block's stored KV, while denoising keeps the base historical context. Commit Forcing improves 60-second VBench Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Its consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, and it achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on 120-second LongLive videos.

2611.01970.title: Knowledge-Guided Floodwater Level Reasoning for Cloud-Edge Collaborative Monitoring
2611.01970.authors: Zhengshu Zhou, Shaoyu Wang, Ziyi Geng, Lu Tao, Qian Long
2611.01970.abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints.
