This stems from a lack of output diversity: existing alignment methods can collapse to a single majority-preferred response, making additional samples redundant. In contrast, our approach preserves output diversity and achieves the optimal test-time scaling rate. In particular, we propose a family of symmetric multi-player alignment games and prove that any symmetric Nash equilibrium policy of the $(k+1)$-player alignment game achieves the optimal $(k,\frac{k}{k+1})$-robust alignment. Finally, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for self-play learning dynamics in these games and extend the framework to opponents that also generate multiple responses.

2601.11016.title: Contextual Distributionally Robust Optimization with Causal and Continuous Structure
2601.11016.abstract: WWe propose a framework for contextual distributionally robust optimization (DRO) that considers the causal and continuous structure of the underlying distribution, and we develop interpretable and tractable decision rules. We first introduce the causal Sinkhorn discrepancy (CSD), an entropy-regularized causal Wasserstein distance that encourages continuous transport plans while preserving causal consistency. We then formulate a contextual DRO model with a CSD-based ambiguity set, termed Causal Sinkhorn DRO (Causal-SDRO), and derive its strong dual reformulation, where the worst-case distribution is characterized as a mixture of Gibbs distributions. To obtain an (infinite-dimensional) optimal policy, we propose a soft regression forest (SRF) decision rule: it preserves the interpretability of classical decision trees while being fully parametric, differentiable, and Lipschitz-smooth, enabling intrinsic interpretation from both global and local perspectives. To solve Causal-SDRO with parametric decision rules, we develop an efficient stochastic compositional gradient algorithm that converges to an $\varepsilon$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ iteration complexity and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-5})$ sample complexity. Finally, numerical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance and interpretability of our method.

2601.20245.title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
2601.20245.abstract: AI assistance produces significant productivity gains across professional domains, particularly for novice workers. Yet how this assistance affects the development of skills required to effectively supervise AI remains unclear. Novice workers who rely heavily on AI to complete unfamiliar tasks may compromise their own skill acquisition in the process. We conduct randomized experiments to study how developers gained mastery of a new asynchronous programming library with and without the assistance of AI. We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without delivering significant efficiency gains on average. Participants who fully delegated coding tasks showed some productivity improvements, but at the cost of learning the library. We identify six distinct AI interaction patterns, three of which involve cognitive engagement and preserve learning outcomes even when participants receive AI assistance. Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill formation -- particularly in safety-critical domains.

2601.21285.title: Zenith: Scaling up Ranking Models for Billion-scale Livestreaming Recommendation
2601.21285.authors: Ruifeng Zhang, Zexi Huang, Zikai Wang, Ke Sun, Bohang Zheng, Yuchen Jiang, Zhe Chen, Zhen Ouyang, Huimin Xie, Phil Shen, Junlin Zhang, Yuchao Zheng, Wentao Guo, Qinglei Wang
2601.21285.abstract: Accurately capturing feature interactions is essential in recommender systems, and recent trends show that scaling up model capacity could be a key driver for next-level predictive performance. While prior work has explored various model architectures to capture multi-granularity feature interactions, relatively little attention has been paid to efficient feature handling and scaling model capacity without incurring excessive inference latency. In this paper, we address this challenge by presenting Zenith, a scalable and efficient ranking architecture that learns complex feature interactions with minimal runtime overhead. Zenith uses Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) as a common capacity-scaling mechanism across feature interaction and long-sequence encoding, while adapting its parameterization to each token regime. The Feature Interaction Unit applies tokenwise attention and SMoE to a small, fixed set of high-dimensional Prime Tokens. In contrast, the Sequence Encoding Unit processes thousands of temporal tokens with SMoE-based query, key, and value projections and an SMoE-based feed-forward network. For the livestreaming-specific delayed-feedback problem, Zenith's Target Modeling Unit efficiently connects timely but incomplete short-horizon supervision with complete long-horizon supervision. Its real-world effectiveness is demonstrated through deployment on TikTok Live, a leading online livestreaming platform that attracts billions of users globally. Our online A/B test achieves gains of 9.93% in Quality Watch Session / User and 8.11% in Quality Watch Duration / User.

2601.21522.title: More Bang for the Buck: Improving the Inference of Large Language Models at a Fixed Budget using Reset and Discard (ReD)
2601.21522.authors: Sagi Meir, Tommer D. Keidar, Noam Levi, Shlomi Reuveni, Barak Hirshberg
2601.21522.abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) on verifiable tasks is usually measured by pass@k, the probability of solving a problem correctly at least once in k trials. At a fixed budget, a more suitable metric is coverage@cost, the average number of unique problems solved as a function of the total number of attempts. We connect the two metrics and show that the empirically-observed power-law behavior in pass@k leads to a sublinear growth of the coverage@cost (diminishing returns). To solve this problem, we propose Reset-and-Discard (ReD), a query method of LLMs that increases coverage@cost for a given budget, regardless of the pass@k form. Moreover, given a pass@k, we can quantitatively predict the savings in the total number of attempts using ReD. If pass@k is not available for the model, ReD can infer its power-law exponent. Experiments across coding (HumanEval), math (GSM8K), and reasoning (MMLU-Pro) benchmarks, as well as real GitHub issues solved by a coding agent (SWE-bench Lite), demonstrate that ReD substantially reduces the required attempts, tokens, and USD cost to reach a desired coverage, while also offering an efficient way to measure inference power-laws. ReD's advantage is maintained for imperfect verifiers.

2602.01541.title: Toward Cognitive Supersensing in Multimodal Large Language Model
2602.01541.authors: Boyi Li, Yifan Shen, Yuanzhe Liu, Yifan Xu, Jiateng Liu, Xinzhuo Li, Zhengyuan Li, Jingyuan Zhu, Yunhan Zhong, Fangzhou Lan, Jianguo Cao, James M. Rehg, Heng Ji, Ismini Lourentzou, Xu Cao
2602.01541.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in open-vocabulary visual understanding, yet they often struggle with cognitive visual reasoning tasks that require maintaining, transforming, and simulating abstract visual states. Existing approaches primarily scale Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in language, forcing inherently spatial or visual computations into discrete text tokens. We introduce Cognitive Supersensing, a training paradigm that equips MLLMs with latent visual reasoning by integrating a Latent Visual Imagery Prediction (LVIP) head that progressively learns refined visual latent states aligned with the evolving reasoning context and target answer, thereby providing a structured visual grounding signal for internal reasoning. We further introduce a reinforcement learning stage that optimizes rationale trajectories using both answer evidence and LVIP-based latent grounding, encouraging reasoning paths that remain visually consistent. To evaluate the cognitive capabilities of MLLMs, we present CogSense-Bench, a comprehensive visual question answering (VQA) benchmark assessing five cognitive dimensions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MLLMs trained with Cognitive Supersensing significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines on CogSense-Bench and exhibit superior generalization on out-of-domain mathematics and science VQA benchmarks, suggesting that internal visual imagery may be key to bridging the gap between perceptual recognition and cognitive understanding. Causal analyses through noise injection, latent patching, and linear probing show that LVIP states progressively encode task-relevant visual structure and influence downstream answer probabilities, supporting their role as active reasoning signals.

2602.05605.title: Shiva-DiT: Residual-Based Differentiable Top-$k$ Selection for Efficient Diffusion Transformers
2602.05605.authors: Jiaji Zhang, Hailiang Zhao, Jiaju Wu, Ruichao Sun, Xinkui Zhao, Shuiguang Deng
2602.05605.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are costly at high resolution because self-attention scales quadratically with token sequence length. Existing pruning methods do not jointly provide end-to-end learnability, low training overhead, and deterministic token counts for predictable token-dependent computation. We propose Shiva-DiT, based on Residual-Based Differentiable Top-k Selection. Its forward pass executes hard top-k selection, while a residual-aware straight-through estimator propagates gradients to both token scores and the budget k without evaluating a second backbone path. A Context-Aware Router and Adaptive Ratio Policy learn layer- and timestep-dependent retention schedules under a target average budget. Experiments on SD3-Medium, Flux.1-dev, and PixArt-{\Sigma} show consistent reductions in FLOPs and measured latency. On SD3-Medium, Shiva-DiT provides four fidelity-latency operating points and reaches a 1.54x wall-clock speedup with competitive fidelity.

2602.13279.title: LLM-Enhanced Rumor Detection via Virtual Node Induced Edge Prediction
2602.13279.authors: Jiran Tao, Cheng Wang, Binyan Jiang
2602.13279.abstract: The rapid proliferation of rumors on social networks poses a significant threat to information integrity. While rumor dissemination forms complex structural patterns, existing detection methods often fail to capture the intricate interplay between textual coherence and propagation dynamics. Current approaches typically represent nodes through isolated textual embeddings, neglecting the semantic flow across the entire propagation path. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) as a structural augmentation layer for graph-based rumor detection. Moving beyond conventional methods, our framework employs LLMs to evaluate information subchains and strategically introduce a virtual node into the graph. This structural modification converts latent semantic patterns into explicit topological features, effectively capturing the textual coherence that has historically been inaccessible to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To ensure reliability, we develop a structured prompt framework that mitigates inherent biases in LLMs while maintaining robust graph learning performance. Furthermore, our proposed framework is model-agnostic, meaning it is not constrained to any specific graph learning algorithm or LLMs. Its plug-and-play nature allows for seamless integration with further fine-tuned LLMs and graph techniques in the future, potentially enhancing predictive performance without the need to modify original algorithms.

2603.00041.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
2603.00041.abstract: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.

2603.00978.title: EraseAnything++: Enabling Concept Erasure in Rectified Flow Transformers Leveraging Multi-Object Optimization
2603.00978.authors: Zhaoxin Fan, Nanxiang Jiang, Daiheng Gao, Shiji Zhou, Wenjun Wu
2603.00978.abstract: Removing undesired concepts from large-scale text-to-image (T2I) and text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models while preserving overall generative quality remains a major challenge, particularly as modern models such as Stable Diffusion v3, Flux, and OpenSora employ flow-matching and transformer-based architectures and extend to long-horizon video generation. Existing concept erasure methods, designed for earlier T2I/T2V models, often fail to generalize to these paradigms. To address this issue, we propose EraseAnything++, a unified framework for concept erasure in both image and video diffusion models with flow-matching objectives. Central to our approach is formulating concept erasure as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem that explicitly balances concept removal with preservation of generative utility. To solve the resulting conflicting objectives, we introduce an efficient utility-preserving unlearning strategy based on implicit gradient surgery. Furthermore, by integrating LoRA-based parameter tuning with attention-level regularization, our method anchors erasure on key visual representations and propagates it consistently across spatial and temporal dimensions. In the video setting, we further enhance consistency through an anchor-and-propagate mechanism that initializes erasure on reference frames and enforces it throughout subsequent transformer layers, thereby mitigating temporal drift. Extensive experiments on both image and video benchmarks demonstrate that EraseAnything++ substantially outperforms prior methods in erasure effectiveness, generative fidelity, and temporal consistency, establishing a new state of the art for concept erasure in next-generation diffusion models.

2603.02531.title: Guidance Ends When Reading Ends: Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance for Diffusion Models through a Hopfield Lens
2603.02531.abstract: Beyond classifier-free guidance, attention-space guidance extrapolates between a strong and a weak attention map within a single forward pass. However, two questions that govern its behavior remain unexamined: along which direction the extrapolation should proceed, and for how many sampling steps it should be applied. The first governs sample quality, and the second governs cost. Interestingly, viewing attention as sparse Hopfield retrieval answers both questions. At every sampling step, the informative direction is the component of the residual parallel to the sparse retrieval output. The guidance acts on the prompt in proportion to the attention mass that image queries assign to text tokens; and since the prompt shapes the image only in the early part of sampling, guidance matters only while the prompt is still being read. Building on this analysis, we propose Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance (ReGA), which extrapolates only along this parallel component and applies the update only over the early steps holding half of the total prompt-attention mass. Extensive measurements inside the attention layers of UNet and MM-DiT backbones confirm both theoretical predictions. Across various backbone models, in multi-step and few-step regimes, ReGA consistently improves text alignment and human-preference scores over existing attention-space guidance methods, while adding as little as 2% inference time on MM-DiT backbones.

2603.05438.title: Planning in 8 Tokens: A Compact Discrete Tokenizer for Latent World Model
2603.05438.authors: Dongwon Kim, Gawon Seo, Jinsung Lee, Minsu Cho, Suha Kwak
2603.05438.abstract: World models provide a powerful framework for simulating environment dynamics conditioned on actions or instructions, enabling downstream tasks such as action planning or policy learning. Recent approaches leverage world models as learned simulators, but its application to decision-time planning remains computationally prohibitive for real-time control. A key bottleneck lies in latent representations: conventional tokenizers encode each observation into hundreds of tokens, making planning both slow and resource-intensive. To address this, we propose CompACT, a discrete tokenizer that compresses each observation into as few as 8 tokens, drastically reducing computational cost while preserving essential information for planning. An action-conditioned world model that occupies CompACT tokenizer achieves competitive planning performance with orders-of-magnitude faster planning, offering a practical step toward real-world deployment of world models.

2603.08856.title: Unpacking Interpretability: Human-Centered Criteria for Optimal Combinatorial Solutions
2603.08856.authors: Dominik Pegler, Frank J\"akel, David Steyrl, Frank Scharnowski, Filip Melinscak
2603.08856.abstract: Algorithmic support systems can return solutions that are optimal but hard to interpret for humans. A given problem can have multiple, equally optimal solutions that differ substantially in how interpretable they are. Yet there is no precise account of what makes one solution more interpretable than another. To identify structural properties associated with interpretability, we studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem (MSSP), in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand. We found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was. The strongest associations were observed for ordered representations and alignment with a greedy heuristic. Compositional simplicity also showed a consistent association. Reaction-time evidence was mixed; the only reliable result was faster responses when heuristic differences were larger. Webcam-based results of aggregate gaze times did not show reliable associations with the three solution properties. In summary, these results ground interpretability (at least in our packing paradigm) in measurable structural properties of solutions. By identifying these properties (simple compositions, ordered representation, and alignment with a heuristic) our findings motivate interpretability-aware optimization and presentation of machine solutions. They also outline a path to quantify trade-offs between optimality and interpretability in allocation and design tasks.

2603.10701.title: AlphaFlowTSE: One-Step Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Conditional AlphaFlow
2603.10701.authors: Duojia Li, Shuhan Zhang, Zihan Qian, Wenxuan Wu, Shuai Wang, Qingyang Hong, Lin Li, Haizhou Li
2603.10701.abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) aims to recover the speech of a specified speaker from a multi-talker mixture using a short enrollment utterance from that speaker. Real conversational applications require both high extraction quality and low-latency inference across complex mixture conditions. Existing generative TSE approaches improve speech fidelity, but diffusion and flow-based models usually rely on multi-step sampling. One-step variants reduce iterative inference cost, yet often require estimating a trajectory coordinate related to the mixing ratio, introducing an additional dependency. We propose AlphaFlowTSE, which formulates TSE as finite-interval transport from the observed mixture to clean target speech. AlphaFlowTSE learns a conditional mean velocity along a mixture-to-target trajectory and uses a JVP-free AlphaFlow objective that combines local trajectory matching with interval-consistent teacher--student supervision. This parameterization supports predictor-free inference while remaining compatible with an optional MR-enabled configuration. At separator NFE$=1$, the MR-enabled configuration attains the highest PESQ, ESTOI, and SI-SDR among the compared one-step systems on Libri2Mix; under predictor-free inference on REAL-T PRIMARY, AlphaFlowTSE yields lower downstream ASR error rates and higher target-speaker similarity.

2603.11045.title: Neural Field Thermal Tomography: A Differentiable Physics Framework for Non-Destructive Evaluation
2603.11045.authors: Tao Zhong, Yixun Hu, Dongzhe Zheng, Aditya Sood, Christine Allen-Blanchette
2603.11045.abstract: Inverse problems for stiff parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the inverse heat conduction problem (IHCP), are severely ill-posed: the forward map rapidly damps high-frequency interior structure before it reaches the boundary. Soft-constrained physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed the PDE as a residual penalty, decouple the diffusivity from the surface data in their standard two-network inverse formulation, and the evaluated variants fit boundary measurements while leaving the interior field essentially untouched. We propose Neural Field Thermal Tomography (NeFTY), a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction. NeFTY represents the unknown diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network, and at every optimization step passes the candidate field through a differentiable implicit-Euler heat solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, so that the simulated temperature satisfies the discretized heat equation up to the solver tolerance. Adjoint gradients propagate the surface reconstruction error back to the network weights at solver-level memory cost, making test-time inversion tractable on a single GPU. Across synthetic 3D benchmarks, NeFTY outperforms soft-constrained PINN variants, a voxel-grid baseline, and classical L-BFGS voxel inversion through the same solver on label-free volumetric recovery, and it transfers to real thermography data, surpassing classical signal-processing baselines in both defect segmentation and depth estimation. Additional details at https://cab-lab-princeton.github.io/nefty/

2604.01083.title: TRACE: Training-Free Partial Audio Deepfake Detection via Embedding Trajectory Analysis of Speech Foundation Models
2604.01083.authors: Awais Khan, Muhammad Umar Farooq, Kutub Uddin, Khalid Malik
2604.01083.abstract: Partial audio deepfakes, where synthesized segments are spliced into genuine recordings, are particularly deceptive because most of the audio remains authentic. Existing detectors are supervised: they require frame-level annotations, overfit to specific synthesis pipelines, and must be retrained as new generative models emerge. We argue that this supervision is unnecessary. We hypothesize that speech foundation models implicitly encode a forensic signal: genuine speech forms smooth, slowly varying embedding trajectories, while splice boundaries introduce abrupt disruptions in frame-level transitions. Building on this, we propose TRACE (Training-free Representation-based Audio Countermeasure via Embedding dynamics), a training-free framework that detects partial audio deepfakes by analyzing the first-order dynamics of frozen speech foundation model representations without any training, labeled data, or architectural modification. We evaluate TRACE on four benchmarks that span two languages using six speech foundation models. In PartialSpoof, TRACE achieves 8.08% EER, competitive with fine-tuned supervised baselines. In LlamaPartialSpoof, the most challenging benchmark featuring LLM-driven commercial synthesis, TRACE surpasses a supervised baseline outright (24.12% vs. 24.49% EER) without any target-domain data. These results show that temporal dynamics in speech foundation models provide an effective, generalize signal for training-free audio forensics.

2604.07126.title: RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
2604.07126.authors: Diyi Liu, Zihan Niu, Tu Xu, Xingchen Zhang, Lishan Sun
2604.07126.abstract: Predicting traffic agent trajectories plays an important role in autonomous driving, traffic operations, transportation safety analysis, etc. Although many deep learning algorithms are devised to predict future agent trajectories, the trajectory prediction problem is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios. Most existing methods are limited by the requirement of graph structures (e.g., Graph Neural Network) or the requirement of manually labeled intentions. In this study, we propose a pure Transformer-based deep learning model for multi-modal trajectory prediction considering temporal dependencies and agent-agent spatial interactions. After encoding the historical trajectories, two parallel decoders are employed to generate trajectories and probabilities on separate decoder tracks. The model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, one highway dataset and the other pedestrian dataset with solid performance. One important insight is that following a ``propose-then-select'' strategy, the agent-agent spatial interactions are only considered for probability estimation instead of trajectory generation. In summary, the proposed model provides a potential direction to design more robust and effective multi-modal trajectory prediction models.

2604.16241.title: BAGEL: Benchmarking Animal Knowledge Expertise in Language Models
2604.16241.authors: Jiacheng Shen, Masato Hagiwara, Milad Alizadeh, Ellen Gilsenan-McMahon, Marius Miron, David Robinson, Emmanuel Chemla, Sara Keen, Gagan Narula, Mathieu Lauri\`ere, Matthieu Geist, Olivier Pietquin
2604.16241.abstract: Large language models perform well on broad knowledge benchmarks, yet their animal-domain competence remains poorly characterized under a consistent protocol. We introduce BAGEL (\textbf{B}enchmarking \textbf{A}nimal knowled\textbf{G}e \textbf{E}xpertise in \textbf{L}anguage models), a 6,822-question multiple-choice benchmark drawn from Wikipedia, Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI), and bioRxiv. It spans encyclopedic species knowledge, ecological interaction inference, and interpretation of animal-focused preprints. Questions are generated automatically and screened by GPT-5.5 using a rubric calibrated on 150 expert-reviewed items; this process is not exhaustive human adjudication. We evaluate 14 models without external retrieval, using model parameters and question-local evidence. Accuracy varies sharply by source and question type: frontier models that excel on Wikipedia and bioRxiv remain comparatively weak on GloBI participant identification, where pooled errors reveal ecological role confusion. A 100-item post-release bioRxiv probe provides preliminary evidence that GPT-5.4's literature performance is not entirely due to verbatim recall, without ruling out broader training exposure. Proprietary checkpoints lead the best open-weight systems overall, but aggregate scores incompletely characterize animal-domain competence.

2604.23351.title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
2604.23351.authors: Houman Mehrafarin, Amit Parekh, Ioannis Konstas
2604.23351.abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computationally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens contain task-solving information. We present a mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K using activation patching: transferring token-level hidden states from an arithmetic CoT generation to a direct-answer run for the same question, then measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy. Across models, patching can elicit generations that lead to correct answers, revealing that individual CoT hidden states can encode sufficient task-solving information even when the original CoT trace is incorrect. This information is more prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs and is unevenly distributed across tokens, concentrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patching from language tokens such as verbs and entities more frequently elicits correct reasoning traces, whereas patches from mathematical tokens more often produce answer-proximal generations that rarely succeed. Further analysis shows that earlier CoT tokens concentrate recoverable information, while later ones require broader search to find the correct answer. Together, these findings show that CoT encodes recoverable, token-level task-solving information, revealing how arithmetic reasoning is represented, accessed, and disrupted.

2604.23750.title: The Override Gap: A Magnitude Account of Knowledge Conflict Failure in Hypernetwork-Based Instant LLM Adaptation
2604.23750.authors: Shuaizhi Cheng, Xiang Shi, Zhiwei Zhang, Mingwei Li
2604.23750.abstract: Hypernetwork-based methods such as Doc-to-LoRA internalize a document into an LLM's weights in a single forward pass, but struggle when the document contradicts pretraining knowledge. We study this override gap through the competition between the pretrained answer margin and the shift induced by the generated adapter. On 194 Gemma conflicts, baseline accuracy falls from 65.3% in the weakest-prior quartile to 16.3% in the strongest. We introduce two training-free methods: Selective Layer Boosting (SLB), which scales the adapter at its highest-activity layers, and Conflict-Aware Internalization (CA), which chooses between standard and stronger adaptation using a short base-model probe. Strong boosting raises Gemma deep-conflict accuracy from 46.4% to 71.0%, with conflict gains also observed on Mistral-7B and Qwen-4B. Matched-norm controls show that both update magnitude and allocation matter: SLB benefits from the generated layer and direction structure, while global scaling is competitive at the same increment budget. CA offers a workload-dependent recall-latency tradeoff, reaching 98.4% novel recall on Gemma while retaining the strong path's conflict accuracy. KID-Bench provides 486 questions spanning novel recall, mixed knowledge, and prior-graded conflicts, with answer-level semantic evaluation.

2604.26774.title: MemOVCD: Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Change Detection via Cross-Temporal Memory Reasoning and Global-Local Adaptive Rectification
2604.26774.authors: Zuzheng Kuang, Honghao Chang, Boqiang Liang, Haoqian Wang, Lijun He, Fan Li, Haixia Bi
2604.26774.abstract: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) seeks to identify semantic changes in bi-temporal remote sensing imagery with text-specified target categories. Representative foundation-model pipelines decode the two timestamps independently before comparing their predictions, leaving cross-temporal evidence unavailable to semantic decoding. Moreover, current patch-wise inference can undermine global semantic continuity, yielding fragmented predictions. To address these limitations, we put forward MemOVCD, a training-free framework which reformulates OVCD as cross-temporal memory-conditioned inference. Specifically, MemOVCD casts bi-temporal analysis as a bidirectional two-frame tracking problem and exploits the memory mechanism of video SAM to propagate semantic candidate regions across timestamps. Their features are pooled and averaged into a local exemplar token. Subsequently, a shared memory, whose number of prototypes is determined by local-exemplar availability, aggregates regional features from the unlabeled target collection. The local and shared tokens are then jointly used to condition the subsequent semantic segmentation. We further devise a global-local adaptive rectification strategy, which adaptively fuses local and global predictions to compensate for incomplete spatial support when processing large images while preserving fine-grained details. MemOVCD and its inductive variant L-MemOVCD show favorable performance on five benchmarks, and ablations and analyses further validate its effectiveness under evaluated settings. Our code will be publicly available.

2604.28123.title: Beyond SFT-to-RL: Pre-alignment via Black-Box On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal RL
2604.28123.authors: Sudong Wang, Weiquan Huang, Xiaomin Yu, Zuhao Yang, Hehai Lin, Keming Wu, Chaojun Xiao, Chen Chen, Wenxuan Wang, Beier Zhu, Yunjian Zhang, Chengwei Qin
2604.28123.abstract: The standard post-training recipe for large multimodal models (LMMs) applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated demonstrations followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, SFT introduces distributional drift that neither preserves the model's original capabilities nor faithfully matches the supervision distribution. This problem is further amplified in multimodal reasoning, where perception errors and reasoning failures follow distinct drift patterns that compound during subsequent RL. We introduce PRISM, a three-stage pipeline that mitigates this drift by inserting an explicit distribution-alignment stage between SFT and RLVR. Building on the principle of on-policy distillation (OPD), PRISM casts alignment as a black-box, response-level adversarial game between the policy and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) discriminator with dedicated perception and reasoning experts, providing disentangled corrective signals that steer the policy toward the supervision distribution without requiring access to teacher logits. While 1.26M public demonstrations suffice for broad SFT initialization, distribution alignment demands higher-fidelity supervision; we therefore curate 113K additional demonstrations from Gemini 3 Flash, featuring dense visual grounding and step-by-step reasoning on the hardest unsolved problems. Experiments on Qwen3-VL show that PRISM consistently improves downstream RLVR performance across multiple RL algorithms (GRPO, DAPO, GSPO) and diverse multimodal benchmarks, improving average accuracy by +4.4 and +6.0 points over the SFT-to-RLVR baseline on 4B and 8B, respectively. Our code, data, and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/XIAO4579/PRISM.

2605.01643.title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction
2605.01643.authors: Rohit Agarwal, Joshua Lin, Mark Braverman, Elad Hazan
2605.01643.abstract: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement, which treats misconduct as a rational response to incentivizes, where actors weigh the expected gain from aligning against the expected loss from being caught. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in foundational language models: an agent trained by RLHF can be modeled as deriving intrinsic reward from producing a persuasive yet incorrect response, while an auditor can be viewed as balancing monitoring (which incurs some cost) against identifying solver misalignment. Therefore, alignment can be viewed as a mechanism design problem, where stronger penalties can deter solver misbehavior but also reduce auditing pressure. Under this framework, we can characterize misalignment as an adversarial post-training problem. While standard post-training optimizes against a stationary reward signal, our mechanism constantly adapts to mitigate reward hacking against a fixed monitor. We formalize this interaction as follows: a principal (e.g., a human) defines a value function over joint alignment outcomes, and a meta-optimizer adaptively chooses granular rewards for the solver and auditor to optimize the principal's value. In particular, we propose a bandit-based meta-optimizer for searching over a discrete set of reward profiles using noisy interaction feedback, and we show from experimental results on Qwen2.5-7B that this mechanism can reduce hallucinations on programming benchmarks by as much as 52\%.

2605.01945.title: PepSpecBench: A Unified Evaluation Benchmark for Peptide Tandem Mass Spectrometry Prediction
2605.01945.authors: Zhiwen Yang, Pan Liu, Yifan Li, Yunhua Zhong, Jun Xia
2605.01945.abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry provides a high-throughput framework for identifying and quantifying proteins in complex biological samples. In computational proteomics, predicting peptide MS/MS spectra is a critical task, enabling downstream applications such as large-scale peptide identification and quantification. While deep learning architectures have substantially improved prediction accuracy, three evaluation challenges obscure the true progress of the field. First, inconsistent data preprocessing and incompatible model output spaces hinder fair model comparison. Second, flawed data splitting strategies can permit hidden sequence leakage and inflate reported performance. Third, existing evaluations typically lack systematic assessment of heterogeneous zero-shot domain shift and robustness to collision energy and precursor charge. To address these challenges, we propose PepSpecBench, a unified benchmark for peptide MS/MS spectrum prediction. The main leaderboard scores all six predictors on a shared b/y fragmention intensity subtask, so their outputs are directly comparable. PepSpecBench standardizes data preprocessing across complementary public datasets, enforces a strict backbone-disjoint splitting strategy to prevent exact backbone overlap across partitions, and evaluates diverse architectures within a shared fragment-ion representation space. It further introduces a heterogeneous zero-shot domainshift suite and metadata perturbation probes to assess robustness and whether models respond to fragmentation-relevant experimental conditions. Across six representative models, we uncover changes in model rankings across training sources and external test subsets, along with differences in their responses to collision-energy and precursor-charge perturbations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zwYang2004/PepSpecBench.

2605.05703.title: Active Learning for Communication Structure Optimization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
2605.05703.authors: Huchen Yang, Xinghao Dong, Dan Negrut, Jin-Long Wu
2605.05703.abstract: Optimizing the communication structure of large language model based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) has been shown to improve downstream performance and reduce token usage. Existing methods typically train on randomly sampled tasks. We show that this optimization is sensitive to the choice of training tasks: downstream accuracy varies widely across random task sets, and adding more random tasks does not consistently improve it. To actively identify the most valuable tasks from a pool of task-answer pairs, we propose an ensemble-based information-theoretic task selection framework. It estimates task informativeness by how much a candidate task changes the distribution over graph parameters, using ensemble Kalman inversion as an efficient and derivative-free approximation of the Bayesian update. The resulting estimator is especially suitable for black-box and noisy multi-agent systems and remains effective with ensembles much smaller than the parameter dimension. To further reduce the number of tasks whose informativeness must be evaluated, we introduce representative pre-selection and surrogate modeling. We validate the framework in benign and adversarial settings and across multiple task formats. It outperforms random training, demonstrating more effective task selection and greater overall cost efficiency.

2605.07395.title: Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts
2605.07395.abstract: Efficient routing across multiple LLMs enables cost-quality tradeoffs by directing queries to the cheapest capable model. Prior work attributes routing headroom to an "unsolvability ceiling", queries no model in the pool can solve. We present a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families. Evaluating with both LLM-as-a-judge and exact-match metrics, we show that a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts: (i) systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness, (ii) truncation under fixed generation budgets, and (iii) output format mismatches. Through dual-judge validation and exact-match grounding, we reduce measured unsolvability across tasks. We introduce a decomposition framework attributing failures to these artifacts, revealing consistent patterns across domains and model families. These artifacts also distort router training signals: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost. We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives. Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated, underscoring the need for reliable evaluation protocols in multi-LLM systems.

2605.07719.title: Mosaic: Efficient CPU--GPU Coordinated Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding
2605.07719.authors: Feiyu Yao, Zhixiong Niu, Xiaqing Li, Yongqiang Xiong, Juan Fang, Qian Wang
2605.07719.abstract: Long-context LLM serving increasingly relies on CPU-resident context KV cache, driven by KV offloading and disaggregated prefill--decode execution. Although block-sparse attention reduces KV access, existing designs remain inefficient: GPU-centralized execution fetches selected KV blocks from CPU memory at each decoding step, making it PCIe-bound, while CPU--GPU partitioned execution places CPU-side sparse attention on the critical path, leaving substantial GPU time idle. This paper presents Mosaic, a CPU--GPU coordinated block-sparse attention system for efficient long-context decoding with CPU-resident context KV. Mosaic builds on three key insights: output-contribution-aware KV budgeting, head-specific and granularity-aware sparse configuration, and cross-device coordinated scheduling for sparse tasks over CPU-resident KV. Guided by these insights, Mosaic integrates a lightweight head-property predictor, a granularity--budget selector, and a priority-based scheduler to automatically configure and coordinate sparse attention, preserving output quality while improving efficiency on heterogeneous architectures. Across 2 models, 3 benchmarks, and 40 tasks, Mosaic preserves near-FULL quality while achieving a better overall quality--efficiency tradeoff than the evaluated baselines. Compared with the best-quality fixed Quest configuration, Mosaic improves TPOT by up to 3.7$\times$. We further validate Mosaic across four hardware configurations and in a large-model multi-GPU deployment.

2605.09887.title: The Geometric Wall: Manifold Structure Predicts Layerwise Sparse Autoencoder Scaling Laws
2605.09887.authors: Eslam Zaher, Maciej Trzaskowski, Quan Nguyen, Fred Roosta
2605.09887.abstract: SAEs operationalise the linear representation hypothesis: they reconstruct model activations as sparse linear combinations of dictionary atoms hypothesised to represent meaningful linear directions. Their reconstruction error varies sharply across layers in ways that existing scaling laws, fitted at a single layer, do not explain. We contend that this variation is the empirical trace of the changing geometric structure of activation manifolds across depth: as their intrinsic dimension and curvature vary from layer to layer, so does the difficulty of approximating them with sparse linear dictionaries, and SAE width-sparsity scaling becomes a layer-dependent function of manifold structure rather than a single universal law. We conduct the first cross-layer SAE scaling study, fitting per-layer scaling-law surfaces to 844 residual-stream Gemma Scope SAE checkpoints spanning all 68 layers of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, and relating the fitted scaling parameters to four geometric summaries of the activation manifold. We find that manifold geometry predicts the per-layer width-scaling exponent in both models, explaining variation that cannot be reliably captured by layer depth alone. A controlled experiment on 150 synthetic manifolds, where intrinsic dimension and curvature vary independently, further reveals two distinct geometric contributions: intrinsic dimension governs the rate at which reconstruction improves with dictionary width, while curvature governs the residual error at the largest trained width. At the six Gemma showcase layers where richer width grids permit identification of an asymptotic floor, the fitted floors follow the same geometric ordering, consistent with the second-order residual that sparse linear approximations of curved manifolds can leave behind. SAEs thus encounter not merely a finite-resource ceiling but a geometric wall set by the manifold they are trying to reconstruct.

2605.12887.title: EcoGEO: Trajectory-Aware Evidence Ecosystems for Web-Enabled LLM Search Agents
2605.12887.authors: Hengwei Ye, Jiasheng Mao, Zhenhan Guan, Zheng Tian
2605.12887.abstract: Web-enabled LLM agents are changing how online information influences search outcomes. Existing Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) studies mainly focus on individual webpages. However, agentic web search is not a single-document setting: an agent may issue queries, crawl pages, follow links, reformulate searches, and synthesize evidence across multiple browsing steps. Influence therefore depends not only on page content, but also on how pages are organized, connected, and encountered along the agent's browsing trajectory. We study this shift through Ecosystem Generative Engine Optimization (EcoGEO), which treats GEO as an environment-level influence problem for web-enabled LLM agents. To instantiate this perspective, we propose TRACE, a Trajectory-Aware Coordinated Evidence Ecosystem. Given a recommendation query and a fictional target product, our method builds a controlled evidence environment that coordinates an agent-facing navigation entry page with heterogeneous support pages. These pages use shared terminology, internal links, and consistent product attributes to introduce, verify, and reinforce the target product. We evaluate our method on OPR-Bench, a benchmark for open-ended product recommendation. Experiments show that it consistently outperforms page-level GEO baselines in Recommendation. Trajectory-level metrics show improved initial target access and additional internal-link browsing, while follow-up-search effects vary across backbones and comparison methods. Together with the multi-page baseline and ablations, these findings support the role of evidence organization in shaping the agent's evidence-acquisition process. Overall, our findings support an ecosystem research paradigm for GEO, where web-enabled LLM agents are studied in relation to the broader evidence environments that guide search, browsing, and answer synthesis.

2605.14291.title: To See is Not to Learn: Protecting Multimodal Data from Unauthorized Fine-Tuning of Large Vision-Language Models
2605.14291.authors: Chengshuai Zhao, Zhen Tan, Dawei Li, Tianlong Chen, Zhiyuan Yu, Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Huan Liu
2605.14291.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) is increasingly accompanied by unauthorized scraping and training on multimodal web data, posing copyright and privacy risks to data owners. Existing countermeasures, such as machine unlearning and watermarks, are inherently post-hoc approaches that act only after intellectual property infringement has already occurred. In this work, we propose MMGuard to empower data owners to proactively protect their multimodal data against unauthorized LVLM fine-tuning. MMGuard generates unlearnable examples by injecting human-imperceptible perturbations that exploit the learning dynamics of LVLMs. By minimizing the training loss, the perturbation creates an optimization shortcut, causing the model to overfit to the noise and thereby degrading downstream performance when the perturbation is absent during inference. To further strengthen this defense, MMGuard introduces a cross-modal binding disruption, shifting LVLM attention to enforce a spurious correlation between the noise and the training target with theoretical guarantees. MMGuard is evaluated against nine open-source LVLMs across six datasets. Our results demonstrate effective, stealthy, and robust protection under white-box, gray-box, and no-box threat models, establishing a mechanistic advantage in proactively defending against unauthorized fine-tuning exploitation.

2605.17789.title: SocialMemBench: Are AI Memory Systems Ready for Social Group Settings?
2605.17789.abstract: Memory systems for AI assistants were built for single-user dialogue, a design mismatched to multi-party social group settings. This matters for the social assistants being built today: group-acting agents in chat platforms, and proactive personal assistants whose model of a user must include their social context. Existing memory benchmarks evaluate dyadic or workplace dialogue; none targets social groups, where memory must anchor facts in shared history rather than professional roles, separate group norms from individual exceptions, and attribute correctly even after a member leaves. We introduce SocialMemBench, a benchmark of human-verified synthetic social group networks across five archetypes and three size tiers (4-30 members), with 430 personas and 1,031 QA pairs across nine question categories. Our evaluation exposes five failure modes, framed as testable hypotheses, and we provide evidence on two through the research probes Subject-Mem and SMG. Our results support three connected takeaways. First, social-group memory must preserve distinctions that ordinary fact recall misses, such as who dissented from a decision and what one member knows about another. Second, across 43 networks the four evaluated frameworks (Mem0, LangMem, Graphiti, Cognee) score 0.12-0.18, well below uncompressed retrieval (0.346) and full context (0.370) with the same answerer, and changing the answerer or retrieval budget does not close the gap. Third, explicitly representing social information mitigates specific failure modes but leaves others open: Subject-Mem targets single-stream conflation, lifting attribution from 0.25-0.46 to 0.78, and SMG targets norm-individual conflation, lifting group-decision accuracy to 0.70, while the other three modes remain open. We release the dataset, the evaluation pipeline with both research probes, and the audit viewer as a testbed for social-memory research.

2605.18797.title: Simply Stabilizing the Loop via Fully Looped Transformer
2605.18797.authors: Rao Fu, Zixuan Yang, Jiankun Zhang, Jing Ma, Hechang Chen, Yu Li, Yi Chang
2605.18797.abstract: Scaling model performance typically requires increasing model size. Looped Transformer (LT) offers a parameter-efficient alternative by repeatedly reusing the same Transformer blocks, converting additional computation into performance gains without increasing the parameter count or context length. However, increasing the number of loop iterations makes LT increasingly difficult to optimize, often leading to gradient oscillation, residual explosion, and training collapse. We propose the Fully Looped Transformer (FLT), a simple, parameter-free redesign that addresses these problems without adding learnable parameters or imposing specially designed optimization constraints. FLT combines a Fully Looped Architecture, which exposes the recurrent state to every layer, with Attention Injection, which controls recurrent information flow through the existing attention module. These modifications enable FLT to train stably through 12 loops in our tested configurations, while baseline looped models enter high-loss regimes. In the Base-size, 6-loop setting, FLT improves downstream-task accuracy by 14.9\% relative to the original LT. Fixed-loop checkpoint evaluations further show that performance improves as inference depth approaches the trained depth, even without randomized loop-count training, revealing a depth-aware test-time compute interface. Extending this interface beyond the trained range is a promising research direction.

2605.22738.title: Proxy-Based Approximation of Shapley and Banzhaf Interactions
2605.22738.authors: Santo M. A. R. Thies, Hubert Baniecki, R. Teal Witter, Eyke H\"ullermeier, Maximilian Muschalik, Fabian Fumagalli
2605.22738.abstract: Shapley and Banzhaf interactions capture the complex dynamics inherent in modern machine learning applications. However, current estimators for these higher-order interactions trade off between speed and accuracy. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProxySHAP. ProxySHAP reconciles the high sample efficiency of tree-based proxy models with a situational residual correction recovering consistency. On a theoretical level, we derive a polynomial-time generalization of interventional TreeSHAP that computes exact interaction indices for tree ensembles, thereby bypassing exponential tree-depth dependencies in prior methods. Furthermore, we formally analyze the residual adjustment strategy, characterizing the specific conditions under which Maximum Sample Reuse (MSR) corrects proxy bias without its variance scaling exponentially with interaction size. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that ProxySHAP sets a new state-of-the-art standard for approximation quality, including in large-scale applications with thousands of features. By achieving the lowest error in both small- and large-budget regimes, ProxySHAP significantly outperforms the prior best estimators ProxySPEX and KernelSHAP-IQ, while also delivering superior performance on downstream explainability tasks.

2605.22973.title: Worse than Random: The Importance of a Baseline for Unsupervised Feature Selection -- Extended Version
2605.22973.authors: Muhammad Rajabinasab, Michael E. Houle, Oussama Chelly, Arthur Zimek
2605.22973.abstract: Many novel unsupervised feature selection methods are proposed each year, yet their empirical evaluation is limited to supervised and unsupervised evaluation metrics computed on selected datasets, along with comparisons to existing methods. However, in the absence of an established evaluation baseline, it is difficult to determine the value added to the existing literature by each of these methods, and how effective their underlying approaches are. In this evaluation study, we are using random feature selection as a baseline for evaluating unsupervised feature selection methods. While a random selection of features might seem to be a rather weak baseline, we show in this evaluation study that many of the state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised feature selection are outperformed by random feature selection in both performance and efficiency. Accordingly, we emphasize the strict requirement of considering random feature selection as a baseline in the development process of novel unsupervised feature selection methods, and we encourage the community to develop better evaluation measures for feature selection. Both would help to ensure consistent improvement and realistic assessment.

2605.23986.title: MemForest: Write-Efficient Agent Memory with Decoupled Extraction and Hierarchical View Maintenance
2605.23986.authors: Han Chen, Zining Zhang, Wenqi Pei, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich, Wei Wu, Hongbao Zhang, Sen Gao
2605.23986.abstract: Long-lived LLM agents maintain semantic views, such as fact records, profiles, and summaries, over a growing interaction history. Maintaining these views is a principal cost of agent memory: ingesting one conversation takes 15--53 minutes with leading memory systems, and most of this time lies on chains of dependent LLM calls that additional LLM capacity barely shortens. Because an LLM-generated view admits no delta rule, existing designs either serialize writes around revising views or give up fresh, reusable views. We present \textbf{MemForest}, which treats every view as a result derived from durable facts and recomputes it only from its children in a time-ordered tree. The dependency depth of view refresh then follows tree height rather than history length. Facts are extracted independently of existing memory, shared ancestors are refreshed once per batch, and independent views refresh in parallel. At query time, links from facts to trees recover details that compact views omit, and materialized interval views are reused for time-range aggregation. Against six released systems, MemForest builds memory \(4.7\times\) faster than EverMemOS on LongMemEval-S and \(8.8\times\) faster on LoCoMo. With Qwen3-30B, it matches EverMemOS on LoCoMo (84.1\%) and attains the highest LongMemEval-S accuracy (81.8\%).

2605.24057.title: Feature Lottery? A Bifurcation Theory of Concept Emergence
2605.24057.abstract: Neural networks learn structured representations at specific points during training, yet pinpointing these transitions usually requires post-hoc, label-dependent metrics. We introduce a bifurcation theory of representation dynamics to detect these moments in real time. By analyzing a passive GMM probe on an evolving encoder, we show that the emergence of structure corresponds to a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation driven by the loss Hessian. Comparing a theoretically predictable zero-crossing ($\beta_c$) with the network's current state ($\beta$) yields a dynamic ratio, $\beta(t)/\beta_c(t)$. Computed solely from hidden states, this ratio is a universal, label-free phase coordinate for representation dynamics. We validate the four transition regimes this coordinate predicts across diverse settings: sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on language models (Pythia), self-supervised learning (CIFAR), and grokking (modular arithmetic). Crucially, under finite dissipation, macroscopic symmetry breaking can lag the initial zero-crossing by orders of magnitude, providing a rigorous dynamical explanation for delayed generalization in grokking. Microscopically, the theory predicts that the bifurcation creates a shared unstable subspace that forces collective symmetry breaking. We call this the \emph{feature lottery} in SAE training: a feature's eventual interpretability is determined very early on. Just $5\%$ into training, early atom purity strongly predicts final purity at convergence: atoms in the top $10\%$ at the $5\%$ mark reach a final POS purity of $0.82$, versus $0.47$ for the bottom $10\%$ and $0.22$ for chance. Beyond explaining how concepts emerge, $\beta/\beta_c$ is a practical early-warning indicator of training health, capturing the onset of usable structure, the crystallization of feature identities, and the beginning of representation collapse many epochs before downstream metrics react.

2605.24743.title: Bilevel Optimization of Synthetic Trajectories for Multi-Turn LLM Fine-Tuning
2605.24743.authors: Shresth Verma, Mauricio Tec, Cheol Woo Kim, Kai Wang, Milind Tambe
2605.24743.abstract: While LLMs excel at single-turn generation, they struggle with long-horizon, multi-turn interactions. Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers a scalable approach, yet its performance hinges on the availability and quality of multi-turn trajectory data. A common remedy is to augment training with synthetic trajectories generated by LLMs or simulators, but synthetic data is highly heterogeneous in quality, and naively treating all trajectories as equally informative can degrade performance. We propose BOOST, a bilevel optimization framework where the inner level trains the LLM on reweighted data and the outer level trains a lightweight reweighting head on held-out real validation tasks, assigning continuous trajectory-level weights without requiring an external judge. To ground this approach, we derive a PAC-Bayesian bound revealing a three-way trade-off: synthetic data increases diversity but risks task-shift, while concentrating weight on high-quality trajectories improves empirical performance at the cost of effective sample size. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms multiple baselines. Analysis reveals it upweights synthetic trajectories that align with the real data distribution and exhibit higher qualitative merit.

2605.26910.title: EEG-FM-Audit: A Systematic Evaluation and Analysis Pipeline for EEG Foundation Models
2605.26910.authors: Xianheng Wang, Yige Yang, Damien Coyle
2605.26910.abstract: EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs) show potential for learning generalized representations from heterogeneous EEG signals. However, existing studies exhibit three critical limitations: opaque model tuning, unverified contributions of complex learning paradigms to EEG-FMs, and a limited understanding of the neurophysiological features that FMs rely on to make decisions. To address these challenges, we propose EEG-FM-Audit, a systematic evaluation and diagnostic pipeline comprising three modules: (1) a fairness-calibrated benchmarking protocol ensuring fair comparisons through model-tailored hyperparameter optimization for EEG-FMs and supervised baselines; (2) three paradigm-level ablation workflows isolating contributions of heterogeneous data scale, self-supervised pretraining, and pretrained linguistic priors; and (3) a neurophysiological probing (NPP) framework exploring whether FMs leverage valid EEG features. Extensive experiments across four leading EEG-FMs and five supervised models on four datasets reveal that well-tuned supervised baselines can match or outperform tuned FMs in some cases, despite requiring significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, ablation analysis indicates that FM pre-training is indispensable for data-scarce downstream tasks, whereas the contribution of pre-trained linguistic components depends heavily on model architecture. Finally, NPP analysis shows that FMs generally extract the established temporal, spatial, and spectral characteristics of the evaluated datasets, establishing a systematic diagnostic benchmark for assessing EEG-FMs.

2605.27404.title: Smaller, Younger, and More Visible? AI-Assisted Writing, Scientific Team Composition, and the Visibility of Scientific Knowledge
2605.27404.authors: Mingze Zhang, Haoyang Wang, Yi Bu, Star Xing Zhao, Meijun Liu
2605.27404.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping scholarly communication, yet little is known about how AI-assisted writing relates to the organization and visibility of scientific knowledge production. This study examines the associations between AI-modified text, publication-team characteristics, and scholarly visibility. Drawing on 144,930 full-text articles and reviews from the PLoS family and the Nature Portfolio published between 2020 and 2025, we use a novel text-based detection approach to estimate AI usage scores as indirect indicators of AI-assisted writing. These scores do not directly measure actual AI use in academic writing but provide indirect signals of AI-assisted writing. We focus on two dimensions of scholarly communication: the production and dissemination of scientific knowledge. The former is reflected in two team characteristics, while the latter is measured by short-term citations. We examine the associations of AI usage scores with team academic age, team size, and citations received within 365 days of publication. Using descriptive comparisons, multivariate OLS, quantile, and Poisson regressions, and propensity score matching, we find that higher AI usage scores are associated with lower average team academic age and smaller publication teams, although the negative association with team size is weaker in the Nature Portfolio. Higher AI usage scores are also positively associated with one-year citation counts. Furthermore, higher AI usage scores are associated with a weaker visibility advantage for larger teams.

2606.00125.title: MusicRec: Audio, Lyrics, and Engagement Feature Enrichment for Music Recommendation
2606.00125.authors: Srikar Prabhas Kandagatla, Sreehitha R. Narayana, Chandana Magapu, Swetha Mohan, Shamanth Kuthpadi Seethakantha, Hongjie Chen, Ryan A. Rossi, Franck Dernoncourt, Nesreen Ahmed
2606.00125.abstract: Music recommendation systems typically treat songs as opaque tokens, relying on interaction histories that overlook semantic or acoustic content. Prior LLM-augmented, multimodal, and text-enhanced sequential recommenders partially combine semantic, acoustic, or engagement signals, and none jointly model all three within a unified LLM-based framework grounded in song content. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework for session-based music recommendation that enriches the LastFM-1K dataset with three complementary signals: (1) audio and lyric embeddings from pretrained music and text models, (2) LLM-generated semantic metadata using the MGPHot schema, and (3) listening completion ratios. We validate the generated metadata against human MGPHot annotations across all 58 attributes. We extend the E4SRec framework with multimodal features, ItemID encoder backbones including SASRec, BERT4Rec, and GRU4Rec, and LLM backbones including LLaMA-2-13B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3-70B across zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. In addition, we evaluate four multimodal fusion strategies, benchmark five audio and five lyric encoders, and compare Spotify audio attributes with LLM-generated MGPHot metadata. Our experiments show that content-based features improve over ID-only baselines by up to 95% in Recall and 79% in NDCG, with the largest gains when the ItemID baseline is weakest. Fine-tuning substantially improves over zero-shot, after which the best audio or lyric setup outperforms the ID-only baseline for every backbone. Naive multimodal fusion does not always yield additive improvements, highlighting challenges in cross-modal integration, while structured LLM-generated metadata proves more useful than Spotify audio attributes. We release a large-scale multimodal benchmark for music recommendation research.

2606.04320.title: OpenRFM: Democratizing Frontier Predictive Intelligence on Relational Data
2606.04320.authors: Zhikai Chen, Junyu Yin, Jialiang Gu, Siheng Xiong, Xiaoze Liu, Ruowang Zhang, Keren Zhou, Kai Guo
2606.04320.abstract: Relational databases hold most enterprise data, and predicting on them has long required hand-written feature joins and a model trained for each task. Relational foundation models (RFMs) remove this per-task engineering by predicting on an unseen database from a few labelled examples in one forward pass. However, the strongest RFMs are closed, and open RFMs pre-trained on synthetic data lag far behind. Prior work attributes this gap to the lack of real pre-training data. We find that much of this gap comes from an incomplete synthetic prior and from a sparse context. Existing synthetic priors lack history-dependent labels, so models pre-trained on them do not learn the temporal and relational dynamics behind real tasks. A bounded context also often misses the evidence that a task needs. We present OpenRFM, an open recipe for building an RFM from synthetic databases alone, whose data generator, model and training code are all open. OpenRFM has three components. (1) A relational adapter, pre-trained on synthetic event streams with history-dependent labels, encodes the sampled context of each entity into a feature row and performs in-context learning along the relation axis, over the history of the entity and its related entities. (2) A frozen tabular foundation model predicts from labelled support rows and performs in-context learning along the batch axis. (3) An optional harness, which an LLM agent builds for each task, rewrites the schema so that the evidence a task needs enters the bounded context. On 32 benchmark tasks, OpenRFM achieves the best mean rank, 3.00 against 3.63 for RelAgent and 5.34 for KumoRFM-2. The code is available at https://github.com/Quant-Spirit/openrfm.

2606.04382.title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
2606.04382.abstract: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlledvocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We introduce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Princeton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unanimous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the underlying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both exact and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted embedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uniform, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.

2606.04493.title: Smooth Inliers, Erratic Outliers: Frequency-Aware Mamba for Two-View Correspondence Learning
2606.04493.authors: Zhihua Wang, Yifeng Gao, Yunhao Feng, Rui Pan, Zhouyuan Ma, Baiheng Zhao, Zixing Chen, Yanping Li, Yizhang Liu, Xingjun Ma
2606.04493.abstract: When shown matches between two photographs of the same cathedral, people can tell at a glance which ones are wrong: a window matched to its look-alike jumps against its neighbors, while correct matches shift together. Two-view correspondence learning, also called correspondence pruning, asks a network to make this judgment for thousands of candidate matches, most of which are wrong. Mamba, a fast sequence model, now drives strong pruners, but it reads the matches as a plain sequence, and whether its scan can capture such agreement is unclear. We propose SFMambaNet, which scans the matches cluster by cluster, so that correct matches vary slowly along the sequence while wrong ones stay erratic, and filters the scanned features with learnable frequency-domain gates between its forward and backward passes. On camera pose estimation, outlier removal and homography estimation, we find that SFMambaNet outperforms spatial-domain Mamba baselines with about two million parameters. Contrary to the usual expectation that such gains come from extra capacity, we find that a parameter-free low-pass filter beats point-wise layers as large as the gates. The learned gates turn low-pass on their own and make the scan far less sensitive to how the matches are shuffled. Together, these results show that frequency is a natural language for describing agreement between correspondences, with implications for other sequence models that must read unordered sets, such as point clouds and graphs.

2606.04987.title: DeliChess: A Multi-party Dialogue Dataset for Deliberation in Chess Puzzle Solving
2606.04987.authors: Xiaochen Zhu, Georgi Karadzhov, Tom Stafford, Andreas Vlachos
2606.04987.abstract: Multi-party dialogue is a critical setting for studying collaborative reasoning and decision-making, yet existing datasets rarely focus on structured, reasoning-intensive tasks. We introduce DeliChess, a dataset of group deliberation dialogues in which participants collaboratively solve multiple-choice chess puzzles. Participants first answer independently, then engage in multi-party deliberation and revise their individual answers. The dataset comprises 107 sessions containing 321 puzzle discussions across 24 unique positions, with full transcripts, pre- and post-deliberation choices, and utterance-level annotations of communicative function, epistemic stance, and usefulness in supporting deliberation. Our analyses show that greater diversity in initial solution quality is associated with larger gains, while answer trajectories reveal how deliberation can recover, discover, or lose strong answers. Cases in which groups surpass every independent answer are associated with sustained reasoning and epistemic openness. We further propose a diagnostic action-selection task: the tested LLMs show limited exact agreement with human-attested helpful actions, while ranked predictions reveal partial alignment. Overall, our dataset provides a testbed for modelling group reasoning, dialogue dynamics, and conditions for effective deliberation.

2606.05737.title: Let It Be Simple: One-Step Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
2606.05737.authors: Yitong Chen, Shiduo Zhang, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu
2606.05737.abstract: One-step generation from standard diffusion or Flow-Matching training is rarely effective for text-to-image or video generation without distillation or specialized one-step objectives. We find that VLA action generation behaves strikingly differently. Biasing only the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong one-step policies across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and real-world robot tasks. Moreover, for open-source VLA models with different architectures, simply replacing iterative decoding with a single forward pass often performs comparably to the original multi-step decoding on benchmarks such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv. We attribute this difference to the condition-target structure of VLA generation, which is closer to image-to-text than text-to-image: rich observations strongly constrain a comparatively compact target. We formalize this intuition through the irreducible velocity loss $R_v(t,c)$ of standard Flow Matching, which becomes much smaller toward the noise endpoint for VLA, whereas image-generation models usually exhibit a U-shaped profile. The geometry induced by the learned generative map shows the same contrast: the Jacobian of this map with respect to the initial noise has a substantially smaller largest singular value for action generation than for image generation. Together, these results suggest that VLA's condition-target structure makes one-step generation unusually accessible to standard Flow Matching. Code and training configurations for this paper are available at https://github.com/bondtesty/let-it-be-simple.

2606.06479.title: Pretraining Recurrent Networks without Recurrence
2606.06479.abstract: Training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) requires assigning credit across long sequences of computations. Standard backpropagation through time (BPTT) addresses this problem poorly: it is sequential in time, limiting parallelism, and suffers from vanishing or exploding gradients, making long-range associations difficult to learn. We propose Supervised Memory Training (SMT), a method for training nonlinear RNNs that sidesteps recurrent credit propagation entirely by reducing RNN training to supervised learning on one-step memory transition labels $(m_t, x_{t+1}) \rightarrow m_{t+1}$. SMT acquires these memory labels by training a Transformer-based encoder on a predictive state objective--retaining only information from the past necessary to predict the future. By decoupling what to remember from how to update memory, SMT enables time-parallel RNN training with a stable $O(1)$ length gradient path between any two tokens--without ever unrolling the RNN. We find that SMT outperforms BPTT when pretraining various RNN architectures on tasks like language modeling and pixel sequence modeling. SMT enables nonlinear RNNs to better capture long-range dependencies and train in parallel, potentially unlocking the scaling of models that build temporal abstractions of past experience.

2606.07527.title: Post-training is (Massive) Supervised Learning
2606.07527.authors: Michael Hassid, Yossi Adi, Roy Schwartz
2606.07527.abstract: The prevailing paradigm for training LLMs has evolved to rely on a massive post-training phase consisting of SFT and RL. In this position paper, we argue that this methodology effectively marks a reversion to the ``pre-train then fine-tune'' approach of the BERT era, explicitly tailoring models to the desired behaviors and specific benchmarks on which they are evaluated. We begin with a historical overview of LLMs, describing the different phases of the LLM evolution. We argue that the current landscape is remarkably similar to the early days of LLMs, where task performance heavily relied on fitting the models to in-distribution datasets. To empirically demonstrate this, we compare pre-trained models to randomly initialized ones, by fine-tuning both variants on modern reasoning datasets and evaluating them on competitive math and code benchmarks. We show that models post-trained from scratch yield highly non-trivial performance. Our findings suggest that current post-training methodologies function primarily as a distribution-fitting mechanism. We finish by positing that developing generally capable models and systems requires moving beyond extensive post-training for predefined behaviors, shifting instead toward training procedures where models ``learn how to learn''.

2606.08777.title: How Many Counterfactuals Does It Take? Probing VLM Hallucinations Through Circuits and Causal Effects
2606.08777.authors: Abhivansh Gupta, Simardeep Singh, Advika Sinha, Shreyansh Modi, Akshat Tomar
2606.08777.abstract: Visual Language Models (VLMs) are known to produce hallucinated predictions that are not grounded in visual evidence, yet existing approaches lack a principled understanding of how robust such predictions are under counterfactual perturbations. In this work, we study the sample complexity of counterfactual robustness for hallucinated outputs in VLMs. We define a causal influence metric based on log-probability differences between factual, counterfactual, and activation-patched runs, and use it to characterize the stability of hallucinated predictions. By leveraging circuit discovery techniques (CD-T), we identify model components responsible for these predictions and track their activation differences across counterfactual samples.
